# web-scraping — taking data from a site you don't own

## Finding the data surface

- **Adding a source, or deciding what to parse** — scraping rendered markup is the **last**
  resort. Prefer, in order: the hydration blob a server-rendered app embeds in the page, then
  the JSON/GraphQL endpoint a single-page app fetches its rows from, and only then the markup
  — where you prefer the page's self-describing metadata (JSON-LD, `og:` tags) over element
  positions, because metadata survives a redesign and `.results > div:nth-child(2)` does not.
  Finding that surface on a new site is a one-off reconnaissance job with its own procedure,
  the [`map-a-data-source`](skills/map-a-data-source/SKILL.md) skill.

- **A rendered-snapshot expectation shifting after a re-record** — rendered output is **not
  deterministic**, so treat the shift the way you'd treat a markup change: re-review it, don't
  assume a regression.

- **Learning something non-obvious by probing the service** — write it down in a reference doc
  beside the scripts: endpoints, auth, the field surface, the enum values. Keep it complete
  enough that **nothing needs to re-probe the live service to answer a question**. The
  expensive part of this work is the knowledge rather than the code, and re-probing is slow,
  rate-limited, sometimes blocked, and occasionally the thing that gets you banned.

## Fetching

- **Writing the fetch itself** — browser-like headers, a randomized delay between requests, and
  exponential backoff on retry. Route **all** outbound page/API fetching through a single
  module, so swapping the vendor, the proxy or the credential is one edit with one place to
  test.

- **Deciding whether to retry a failed request** — retry only what can improve. A gateway or
  proxy failure (408, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504) is worth another attempt; any other 4xx is about
  your request and will answer the same way forever.

- **Porting a fetch to a language-level HTTP client** — carry the retry policy across the
  rewrite. `curl --retry` covers exactly that status set and the port silently drops all of it,
  so the first transient 500 the old command would have ridden out kills the run.

- **Setting the retry budget** — attempts times per-attempt timeout, plus the waits, must fit
  inside whatever hard limit kills the process, and the backoff should be injectable so tests
  exercise the retry path without sleeping through it.

- **One item in a batch failing to fetch** — record and continue. Log the reason per item and
  emit a report; one unfetchable item should not abandon the batch.

- **A sandbox refusing the target host** — an agent sandbox is commonly **bot-blocked**, and its
  egress proxy may refuse the host outright. That refusal is policy: **do not route around it**,
  not with a local fetch and not with an ad-hoc workflow spun up to reach the host. Give the
  fetch one sanctioned home — a scheduled job or workflow on a runner, with the credential in
  repository secrets — and let sessions read the committed raw records instead.

- **A fetch that works on your machine and fails from CI** — a 403/400 or a CAPTCHA wall from a
  runner or a sandbox is usually the *datacenter IP* being blocked, not the headers, so tuning
  them is wasted work. **Reaching a commercial rendering proxy** is the standard answer: a
  residential lane clears the IP block, and these services usually execute JavaScript too, so a
  single-page app records real content. Ask it to render, and give it a wait-for-selector when
  the content you want arrives late. A target that stays blocked even through the proxy is
  un-cacheable: say so and stop, rather than hunting for another route.

- **Needing many items from a service with no list endpoint** — no bulk endpoint is not the same
  as no bulk request. GraphQL lets one document alias the same field many times, and many REST
  APIs accept a multi-id parameter. The cap is usually undocumented, so **halve a rejected batch
  and retry** — that keeps batch size a throughput knob and never an accuracy one.

- **A fetch that cannot produce a page at all** — a bot wall, a dead URL, an empty render is a
  dead end, not a pipeline failure: mark the item for a human and **exit successfully**. Failing
  the run converges on the same human signal while also implying the pipeline broke, when in
  fact it correctly declined. The rest of the batch should still land.

## Reading what came back

- **Deciding whether a fetch succeeded** — a 200 is not success. An anti-bot interstitial arrives
  as a normal-looking 200 (or a 403/503) whose body is a challenge page, and caching it stores
  garbage that looks like data. Match the known markers in the first few KB and report it as a
  distinct failure reason.

- **Getting an empty body back** — nothing rendered. Treat it as a failure of that fetch rather
  than as an empty result, and don't retry it: a successful-but-empty response will keep being
  successful and empty.

- **Choosing which field to read** — prefer the authoritative status enum over the summarizing
  convenience boolean, which is routinely wrong: an item can report "not sold out" while its
  status says there is nothing left to sell. Take the enum's legal values from the service's own
  options endpoint rather than from what you happened to see.

- **Filtering rows by a status** — deny-list the bad statuses, don't allow-list the good ones,
  and log the set actually observed. A new status then defaults to usable and shows up in your
  logs, instead of silently dropping rows.

- **Reading a numeric field** — numbers may arrive as strings. Parse; don't assume the JSON type.

- **Reducing a set to its "cheapest" or "first"** — that value can be a special case rather than
  a value. Filter to what the field means before you reduce over it: a zero-priced accessibility
  companion band makes the cheapest ticket for every show free.

## Normalizing what you read

- **Converting an instant to the domain's local time** — instants usually arrive in UTC while
  your domain thinks in local wall-clock. Do the conversion in one function at the ingestion
  boundary and have everything downstream speak local time. Slicing digits out of the string
  files everything an hour off during daylight saving, and **the result looks completely
  plausible** — nothing throws, nothing is empty, the data is simply wrong. Because the failure
  is silent, keep a **known-answer probe**: an item whose correct value you know independently
  (something named after its own time, a figure published elsewhere), checked after every fresh
  pull. "Exactly once" cuts both ways — a stage downstream of the boundary that parses,
  re-offsets or re-reads a stored value as UTC is the same bug from the other end.

- **Taking a "now"** — read it in the domain's zone rather than off the device clock. A reviewer
  in the same zone as the developer cannot see the difference, which is how a device clock
  survives review.

- **Parsing a value whose format is ambiguous** — read it by what the page declares, centrally;
  never per-source, never guessed. A numeric slash date whose parts are both ≤ 12 (`05/07/2026`)
  has no intrinsic answer, so resolve it from a *positive* signal the document gives you (an
  explicit region in `<html lang>` or `og:locale`, a non-English language) and keep the default
  when the signal is absent or region-less, rather than inferring one from the host or the
  venue. Put that resolution in one helper the whole pipeline threads, so a new source cannot
  invent its own reading. A trailing `Z` or `+00:00` is *serialization*, not a claim about the
  subject's zone: it neither supplies the zone nor vetoes deriving one from what the page says
  about the place.

- **Changing the conversion** — it is a **full-snapshot change**. Committed derived data is
  generator output, so the fix isn't done until the raw record is re-run through the new
  conversion and every downstream artifact regenerated. Expect the boundary to move records
  between partitions — items at the end of a day land in the next one, and may fall outside the
  range your day-partitioned files cover — and check that rather than reading it as data loss.

- **Emitting a value your pipeline hasn't reached yet** — missing is its own state: *unknown*,
  never folded into *free*, *empty* or *false*. Sources keep adding rows after your last full
  pass, so gaps are normal and permanent. Carry unknown through the whole stack — omit the key
  rather than emitting a default — and let each consumer render it as its own thing.

## What lands on disk, and when it refreshes

- **Deciding what a fetch writes to disk** — two forms, separated deliberately. The fetched
  artifact (page HTML, raw response pages) is a **cache**: git-ignore it, since it is large,
  regenerable, and not what you reason about. The extracted raw record — the site's own object,
  before any of your normalization — is **committed**, and is the durable source of truth. That
  split buys three things at once: re-deriving your normalized output becomes an **offline**
  operation, so a parser change costs no requests; the committed record doubles as the fixture
  for a self-test of the transform that needs no network; and a field you didn't parse this
  month is still there next month, because you kept the whole object rather than the subset you
  needed at the time.

- **Re-running a fetch that already ran** — **fetch only what's missing**, with an explicit flag
  to force a refresh, so repeat runs are a no-op. Note what "resumable" is measured against: the
  file on disk. On a CI runner that file is durable only once the job's commit step pushes it,
  so a resumable script still loses everything if the runner itself dies. Chunk the work if that
  matters.

- **Scheduling the refresh** — give each field its own pass on the clock it actually moves on.
  The single biggest cost saving in a scraper is noticing that some fields are fixed once
  published, some gain rows daily and some move hourly: re-fetching everything on the fastest
  clock re-learns a static field nightly, thousands of requests for the same answer, and it is
  the part of your traffic most likely to get you blocked.

- **Generating the artifacts downstream of the stored data** — make them a **pure function of
  the stored master**: refresh writes to the master, and everything else regenerates from it.
  Files whose inputs didn't change come back byte-identical and never enter the commit, so the
  diff of a scheduled run is exactly what actually moved.
===README
# web-scraping pack

Declared (opt-in) by a project whose input is **another organisation's website**,
reached without a contract: no support channel, no changelog, no SLA. No
fingerprint — a scraper is ordinary HTTP client code, indistinguishable from a call
to an API the project owns.

Prose plus one skill, and no checks: every rule is about a *remote* service's
behaviour (which field is authoritative, whether an instant is UTC, when a 200 is a
bot wall), none of which is written into repo state in a shape a check could read
without firing on ordinary HTTP code.

## Rules (`RULES.md`)

| Rule | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|---|
| Adding a source, or what to parse | medium | complexity | prose: 90 words |
| A rendered-snapshot expectation shifting after a re-record | medium | correctness | prose: 31 words |
| Learning something non-obvious by probing the service | medium | complexity | prose: 71 words |
| Writing the fetch itself | medium | correctness | prose: 44 words |
| Deciding whether to retry a failed request | medium | correctness | prose: 43 words |
| Porting a fetch to an HTTP client | medium | correctness | prose: 47 words |
| Setting the retry budget | medium | performance | prose: 38 words |

name: map-a-data-source
description: Reconnaissance on a website you want data from but don't control — locate the real data surface (hydration blob, client API, or markup) and write the findings down before any parser exists. Use when adding a new source to a scraper, or when an existing source stops parsing and you suspect the site changed shape.
---

# Map a data source before you parse it

This runs **once per source** (and again when a site is redesigned). Its output is
not code — it is a committed reference doc plus one saved raw payload. Everything
after it is ordinary parsing.

## 1. Fetch one page and look at what came back

Save the raw response of a single representative page to disk and read it. You are
answering one question: **is the data in this document?**

- If the interesting rows are present in the markup, you have a server-rendered page
  — go to step 2.
- If you got a small shell (a few KB of script tags and an empty root), the page is a
  single-page app and the data arrives separately — go to step 3.

## 2. Look for a hydration blob first

A server-rendered app framework almost always embeds the exact object it rendered
from in a script tag with a stable id. Search the saved document for a large inline
JSON payload and find the path to the record you want (it is usually nested a few
levels under a props/data wrapper).

If one exists, **this is the surface**: it is the site's own typed record, one regex
and one JSON parse away, and it does not care about the layout. Save that object,
verbatim, as your first committed fixture.

If there is no blob, the page's self-describing metadata (JSON-LD `<script
type="application/ld+json">`, `og:` meta tags) is the next-best target — it survives
redesigns that break element selectors.

## 3. Find the client API

Identify the request the page makes for its rows. Two ways in, and the second one
matters more than it sounds:

- **Watch the page load** in browser devtools and read the request: URL, method,
  headers, auth, and the response shape.
- **Read the site's own JavaScript bundles.** Fetch the page, extract the script
  `src` paths (mind any asset prefix — the paths in the HTML already carry it),
  download them, and search for the operation names, query documents and field
  selections. For a GraphQL client the embedded query strings unescape into readable
  SDL, giving you the **complete** set of operations and fields the client was built
  against — the authoritative surface, short of introspection.

  This path is worth knowing because it needs **only the public site host**. When the
  API host is blocked from where you are but the site itself loads, reading its
  bundle still tells you exactly what a request would look like. It cannot execute
  anything, so it is not a bypass of the block.

Then note the auth story. A public listing is frequently reachable with anonymous
credentials the client itself ships — the same read access every visitor has. If
reaching the data requires a real account, stop and take that to the owner.

## 4. Probe the shape, not just the happy path

Before declaring the surface mapped, ask these of it explicitly, because each one has
silently corrupted a pipeline that assumed otherwise:

- **Are timestamps UTC or local?** Take one item whose real-world time you can verify
  independently and check.
- **Which field is authoritative for state?** If there is both a status enum and a
  summarizing boolean, find an item where they disagree — there usually is one.
- **What are the enum's legal values?** Take them from the service's own options
  endpoint, not from the sample you happened to pull.
- **Are numbers numbers?** Amounts and counts frequently arrive as strings.
- **Is anything missing from this surface entirely?** A listing endpoint often
  carries flags but no amounts, with the real values behind a separate per-item
  query. Find that out now, not after you've shipped a catalogue of nulls.
- **Is there a bulk form?** If the per-item query has no list variant, check whether
  one *request* can still carry many items (GraphQL aliases, a multi-id parameter).

## 5. Write it down, then stop

Commit a reference doc beside the scripts holding: the endpoint(s) and auth, the
field surface, the enum values, each answer from step 4, and — explicitly — the
questions you could **not** answer and where they'd have to come from. State the
access constraint too: which hosts are reachable from where, and which sanctioned job
is allowed to do the fetching.

The bar: **a later session should be able to write the parser from this doc without
touching the live service.** If it can't, the reconnaissance isn't finished.

21	
22	A skill is `packs/<pack>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` with YAML frontmatter:

25	---
26	name: <name>
27	description: <one tight sentence: what it is + "Use when …" the activity that should load it>
28	metadata:
29	  force-load-on-file-edits-paths:
30	    - "**/Info.plist"
31	---

33	
34	`metadata.force-load-on-file-edits-paths` is optional: include it ONLY for a path-scoped skill
35	(the issue row's Scope says `paths:`). Never use the harness's own `paths:` frontmatter field.
36	Pattern grammar: `**` spans directories, `*`/`?` stay in one segment, `{a,b}` expands, matched
37	against the whole repo-relative path (so `**/Info.plist` = that file at any depth, `functions/**`
38	= a top-level tree). Skill names are global across all packs; the coordinator checked the issue's
39	names are free — use them verbatim. Skill directory name == frontmatter `name`.
40	
41	Caution from the issue: a `paths:` glob that is a GUESS at a member's file naming (e.g.
42	`**/*Audio*.swift`, `**/fetch*.{js,ts}`, `**/*time*`, `**/auth*.{js,ts}`) does not earn a forced
43	scope — prefer a description-only (activity-triggered) skill there, or keep only the platform-fixed
44	names of the row (`manifest.json`, `**/Info.plist`, `**/*.entitlements`, `**/firestore.rules`,
45	`**/template.yaml`, `pubspec.yaml`, `.claudinite-settings.json`, `dev/requirements/**`,

53	   trailing rationale marker `(n)` if it had one (see references below). Where the row says "into
54	   existing <skill>", append a section to that skill instead of creating one. A skill body needs

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

1	---
2	name: writing-pack-prose
3	description: How pack prose is written — RULES.md rules, SKILL.md bodies and check text in a Claudinite pack, local or canon — brevity, structure, triggerability, findability, and the per-pack references doc. Loaded for any edit of a pack's RULES.md or SKILL.md, and when landing a lesson as prose.
4	metadata:
5	  force-load-on-file-edits-paths:
6	    - "**/packs/*/RULES.md"
7	    - "**/packs/*/skills/*/SKILL.md"
8	---
9	
10	# Writing pack prose
11	
12	Whether a candidate *qualifies* as a rule at all, and which mechanism carries it, is
13	[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)'s call — settle it there before writing.
14	
15	**Start from the foundation:** read the "Write each rule" section of
16	[authoring-agent-docs](../../../basics/skills/authoring-agent-docs/SKILL.md) first — its
17	principles (concrete enough to verify, motivation stated, what to do rather than what not to,
18	the right altitude, emphasis reserved) bind pack prose too. This skill is the pack-specific
19	layer on top of them, and doesn't restate them.
20	
21	## The ration
22	
23	Every rule in a `RULES.md` is paid for by every session in every repo that declares the pack,
24	forever, whether or not it ever applies — so prose is rationed, and the ration is small.
25	
26	- **One sentence per rule, near 40 words**: the trigger, the directive, and a consequence
27	  clause only where the rule cannot be applied without it. A candidate that needs a paragraph
28	  to land has not been understood well enough to be a rule yet.
29	- **An extraction pass adds at most two rules.** If more candidates clear the bar, write the
30	  two strongest and drop the rest — they will recur if they were real.
31	- **Split a rule that carries two situations.** Each situation is its own rule with its own
32	  trigger.
33	- A `SKILL.md` loads only when its activity is under way, so it may carry procedure at length —
34	  but it is still rationed by the same test: every line must change what the reader does.
35	  Method, steps and decision points belong there; anything a session must know *without*
36	  loading it belongs in `RULES.md` or a check, and rationale belongs in the references doc
37	  below.
38	
39	## Shape a rule so it fires
40	
41	- **Keying a rule to its trigger** — open with the act the reader is performing, not the state
42	  of the world the rule applies to. Nobody notices that "a value is unknown"; they notice they
43	  are writing an encoder. A rule keyed to a state never fires, because nothing brings the
44	  reader to it.
45	- **Keying a rule the reader reaches while debugging** — name the symptom that sends them
46	  looking ("A fetch to a host you listed failing in-browser"), not the act that caused it. By
47	  the time the rule is wanted the act is over, and the symptom is what they can see.
48	- **Keying a rule that corrects a misconception** — name what the reader wants ("Wanting
49	  `import`/`export` in extension code"), not the wrong move they might make ("Reaching for a
50	  bundler"). Someone who doesn't yet know the move is wrong won't recognise themselves in it.
51	- **Phrasing that trigger** — use the words the reader would use for the situation, and put
52	  them first and in bold, so the rule is findable by scanning the left margin alone.
53	- **Choosing the unit** — one block per situation, not one bullet per rule. A reader arrives
54	  holding a problem, so give them the whole decision in one place rather than a cross-reference
55	  to three neighbouring bullets.
56	- **Splitting a rule that only makes sense after the one above it** — don't. If the subject
57	  needs a "that" pointing back ("Writing that record"), it is a clause of the rule above, not a
58	  situation of its own. Split when a reader could arrive at the second rule without the first.
59	- **Separating the blocks** — one blank line between rules. The block is what a reader lands on,
60	  and an unbroken run of bullets makes them scan lines instead; the separation costs one token.
61	- **Ordering a file of many rules** — past roughly fifteen, group them under headings naming the
62	  surface each concerns, so a reader scans headings before subjects. A flat list that long makes
63	  every bold subject do the work one heading would.
64	- **Grouping that separates two rules which qualify each other** — add an explicit pointer from
65	  the general rule to its exception, or the general one reads as unconditional. That pointer is
66	  the one sentence a rewrite may add that its source didn't have; name it as an addition when
67	  you report the change.
68	- **Ordering the clauses** — the default first, then the `if you can't` fallback, then
69	  `consider` for an optional aid, then the `don't` that the earlier clauses make unnecessary.
70	- **Choosing modality** — grade it per clause and claim no more than the rule needs. Keep
71	  `never` and `always` for the genuinely absolute and reach for `prefer`, `avoid` or `rather
72	  than` otherwise; escalating a `don't` into a `never` changes the rule rather than rewording
73	  it.
74	- **Naming a mechanism** — name the check, helper or skill that owns the mechanics, and stop.
75	  Its parameters, options and failure modes live with it, and restating them here is a copy
76	  that goes stale. The exception is a mechanism you are telling the reader to *run*, below.
77	- **Telling the reader to *run* something** — ship the literal invocation in a fenced block, not
78	  the file's name. The reader is composing a call rather than looking a mechanism up, so a bare
79	  filename buys a probe every time — the `--help` that prints nothing, then the `cat`, then a
80	  hand-built command. (1)
81	- **Closing a block** — say what the other clauses make unnecessary ("don't also comment the
82	  duplication — the guard covers it"), so nobody adds belt-and-braces.
83	- **Keeping an exception** — an exception that changes what the reader would do is part of the
84	  rule; one that only reassures is padding.
85	- **Cutting a rule's prose** — drop rationale that only restates the rule, examples that
86	  re-express it, and mechanics another document owns. Keep the motivation itself: a consequence
87	  the reader needs in order to apply the rule under pressure earns its clause; rationale the
88	  reader doesn't need at act time goes to the references doc below.
89	- **Auditing a file of rules that already exists** — take each rule and ask what a reader would
90	  get wrong without it. Fold the one whose subject points back at its neighbour; cut the one another
91	  pack already carries, the one a check now enforces (keeping only the half the check can't see),
92	  and the one whose mechanism has since been retired — a rule naming code that no longer exists
93	  teaches a world the reader won't find.
94	- **Rewriting an existing rule** — carry the source's own strength forward. A rewrite must not
95	  weaken a rule, and it must not strengthen one either.
96	
97	## The references doc — where a rule's rationale lives
98	
99	A pack keeps **one** `references.md` beside its `RULES.md`, servicing all of the pack's prose
100	files and its checks. It exists for maintenance and review — the periodic pass that asks
101	whether a rule still earns its place needs the reason it was written — never for daily agentic
102	work: no rule sends its reader there, and no session loads it. So it stays in the repo that
103	owns the pack and never vendors: a member mounting a canon pack receives the rules, not the
104	reasoning behind them, and the pass that reaffirms them runs where the pack lives.
105	
106	- **Adding a rule that has a rationale** — write the brief rule in `RULES.md` (or the skill),
107	  and put the reason in `references.md`. End the rule with the bare marker — `… never a
108	  filesystem walk. (3)` — and nothing else: don't name the references file, don't link it,
109	  don't ask the reader to follow anything. Not every rule needs one; a rule whose reason is
110	  self-evident from its consequence clause carries no marker.
111	- **Writing the entry** — one bullet per entry, keyed by the citing file's own namespace:
112	  `- **(RULES-3)** <reason>` for a rule in `RULES.md`, `- **(<skill-name>-3)** <reason>` for a
113	  line in that skill's `SKILL.md`; the marker in the prose file stays the bare `(3)` and
114	  resolves within its own file's namespace. Write the reason so a future review can **reaffirm
115	  the rule from it**: what would have to be true for the rule to be retired.
116	  - A **workaround** explains the issue with not using it, with the evidence (the failing run,
117	    the error, the measured cost).
118	  - A **technology guideline** cites the original documentation it derives from.
119	  - An **owner decision** carries the language of the request that set it.
120	- **Numbering** — numbers are stable identifiers, not positions: the next entry takes its
121	  file's next unused number, a removed entry leaves a gap, and nothing ever renumbers (a
122	  renumber breaks every marker at once). One entry may serve several rules in its file; a rule
123	  may cite several entries (`(3, 7)`).
124	- **A check's rationale** — the entry points at the check, since a declaration admits no
125	  comment and no new key: `- **(check:growth-write-scope)** <reason>`, same reaffirmation
126	  standard. There is no marker on the check side.
127	- **Removing a rule or check** — remove its entry in the same change, unless another rule
128	  still cites it.
129	
130	The `references-integrity` check holds the mechanism together: every marker must resolve to an
131	entry in the pack's own `references.md`, and every `check:` entry must name a check the pack
132	still carries. The `rule-revalidation` task is the mechanism's consumer — it reaffirms
133	referenced rules and checks against their recorded reasons on its weekly pass.
134	
135	## Migrating an existing pack onto the references doc
136	
137	An existing pack — a repo's local pack, or a shared canon pack worked on canon-side (a member
138	never edits the mounted canon) — migrates opportunistically, one pack per pass, whenever a pass
139	is already editing it. An unmarked rule stays valid forever, so there is no fleet sweep to
140	force and no straggler to chase; the check only judges markers that exist.
141	
142	1. **Create `references.md`** beside the pack's `RULES.md` on its first entry, not before.
143	2. **Work each rule**: keep the act-time consequence clause inline; move review-only rationale —
144	   the evidence story, inline issue ids, a cost the reader doesn't need mid-act — into an entry
145	   and end the rule with its marker. Shrink-only on the rules side: a rule may lose review-only
146	   rationale in this pass, never gain text.
147	3. **Recover the missing reasons from history, source-first**: for a rule that states no reason,
148	   read the commit that added it and that commit's PR and issue *before* re-reading the rule —
149	   derive the entry from the source, then diff against what the rule implied. The commit
150	   message, PR body and issue discussion are where this corpus already keeps a rule's evidence.
151	4. **Never invent an entry.** A rule whose reason can't be recovered stays unmarked — an audit
152	   or the `rule-revalidation` pass judges whether it still earns its place; a plausible-sounding
153	   fabricated rationale would let a future review reaffirm a rule on false grounds.
154	5. **Cover the checks** worth reaffirming with `check:` entries the same way, from their `why`
155	   text and their adding commit's PR.
156	
157	## Evidence
158	
159	The commit and its PR remain the archive — dates, session ids, quoted exchanges and the story
160	of the incident live there, never in the rule. What the references doc takes from them is only
161	the **reaffirmable core**: the reason and the minimum evidence a future review needs to re-test
162	it. Keep a measurement inline in the rule only where the number *is* the argument — a cost the
163	reader wouldn't believe stated qualitatively.
164

9	# Writing Claudinite skills
10	
11	A corpus skill is a harness-matched trigger (frontmatter `name` + a tight `description`, plus `force-load-on-file-edits-paths` under `metadata` where an edit of the files it names must not start without it — the PreToolUse guard holds such an edit until the skill is loaded; never the harness's `paths`, which limits when the skill is offered at all) plus the body the agent needs at usage time — well under 500 lines, and nothing a deterministic mechanism could carry instead (the promotion ladder in [engine/checks/DESIGN.md](../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md) decides). 1	# Executable requirements — the framework standard
2	
3	## 1. The layout is the contract
4	
5	- Everything lives under **`dev/requirements/`**: `requirements.md` (the numbered prose spec),
6	  one **top-level folder per kind**, `shared/` for cross-kind infra, and the runners/gates. The
7	  spec file's path is the framework's structural fingerprint — this pack activates on it.
8	- **A requirement line** starts (optionally after a list dash) with a backtick-wrapped dotted
9	  number: `` `4.2` ``. A **leaf** is an id with no finer-numbered child. Parse with one shared
10	  regex (`` ^\s*(?:-\s+)?`(\d+(?:\.\d+)+)` ``) so specs stay drop-in compatible across projects.
11	- **The line is a scannable one-liner; expanded detail collapses.** A leaf in `requirements.md`
12	  reads as a single line the owner skims down the numbered spine on GitHub. Any expansion —
13	  rationale, acceptance notes, edge cases, the owner-verification recipe — lives inside a
14	  collapsed `<details>` block under the line, hidden until the owner expands it. The doc reviews
15	  as a clean spec, not walls of prose; the depth is one click away when wanted, invisible when
16	  not.
17	- **The folder is the kind.** A case's kind is the directory it lives in; the case declares no
18	  kind field. Cases are
19	  `<kind>/cases/<slug>.<leaf-id>.case.<ext>`: a stable feature slug (so retitling a spec section
20	  never forces renames), then the dotted leaf id.
21	- **Artifact expecteds live beside their case** (`<slug>.<id>.png`, `expected/<name>.json`);
22	  failure artifacts (actual/diff renders) go to a gitignored dir, never beside the goldens.
23	- Where the language discovers cases dynamically (Node `require`), the registry walks the
24	  folders; where it cannot (Dart/Flutter), each kind keeps a hand-written `manifest` and **the
25	  gate enforces manifest ⇄ disk equality** — an unregistered case file never runs, so unregistered
26	  must be red.
27	
28	## 2. What the coverage gate checks
29	
30	The bijection gate is one committed test. It must fail on every one of: a leaf no case claims
31	(doc-first red-by-default); a case claiming a non-existent leaf; two cases claiming one leaf; a misnamed case file; a kind directory absent from the registry (or a
32	registered kind with no directory); a manifest out of sync with disk (where manifests exist); an
33	image found in a coded kind's folder (a screenshot cannot verify a gesture or a pure rule); a
34	stray golden no case or step accounts for. Every rule iterates the registry — adding a kind never
35	edits the gate.
36	
37	The gate checks repo state; an interactive feature run also has an *ordering*: after the
38	owner's feature-classified comment, an independent commit updating the spec (no code alongside)
39	precedes the first code commit on the branch. The spec's path defaults to the canonical
40	`dev/requirements/requirements.md`; a project whose spec lives elsewhere (a non-canonical
41	layout, or the pack pulled in via a `requires` from `spec-driven-product`) names it on the pack
42	entry as `config.spec`.
43	
44	## 3. The kind vocabulary
45	
46	Two forces pick a leaf's kind: what can **honestly observe** the assertion, and what gives the
47	**owner the simplest verification**. Prefer the kind whose expected is a **visual the owner checks
48	by sight** — a surface snapshot or a saga storyboard — and whose per-leaf test body is minimal:
49	drive to the state, capture, done, with the golden as the assertion rather than hand-written
50	expectations. Push as many requirements as can honestly be seen onto that visual path — the more
51	of the spec an owner verifies by *looking*, the more of it they actually review. Reserve the coded
52	kinds (behavior, logic) for what an image genuinely cannot see: a gesture's outgoing request, a
53	pure rule. Route each leaf to the kind that can actually see what it asserts:
54	
55	- **surface snapshot** (`popup`, `icon`, `screen`, …): a rendered resting state, pixel-exact
56	  against a committed golden. One golden per leaf, even when several leaves render the same state
57	  — the bijection stays strict.
58	- **behavior**: a driven gesture and its outgoing request/consequence, asserted in code against
59	  the fakes' recordings. No images allowed in the folder.
60	- **logic**: a pure product rule, a coded `verify()` importing shipped code.
61	- **saga** (§4): a multi-step story as a golden storyboard.
62	- **per-project kinds** where the product's value is breadth or crosses tiers: a per-target
63	  `extractor`/`support` kind (one case per supported external target, proven on committed real
64	  samples), a `server` kind (the boundary's half of a two-tier rule, against the real handler).
65	- **heavy/e2e singleton**: "the product loads in the real environment" — one case, its own lane,
66	  never in the default loop.
67	
68	## 4. Sagas: stories as storyboards
69	
70	Single frames prove states; **sagas prove transitions and causality** — what arriving, acting, or
71	time passing *changes*. Use a saga when the requirement is the story ("a message sent before I
72	arrived never appears; one sent after I arrived does"), not decomposable into independent resting
73	states without losing the claim.
74	
75	- A saga case is an ordered list of **steps**; each step = a caption plus an action against the
76	  fake world; after each step the runner captures one golden frame `<slug>.<id>.step-NN.png`.
77	- The **caption narrates the story** in user terms — captions surface in the gallery.
78	- One saga = one leaf; the frames are that one case's expected (all frames pixel-exact, same
79	  ownership rules as any golden). Keep sagas to 3–6 frames; a longer story is usually two sagas.
80	- Saga steps drive the **same real entry point** as every other kind (the shipped app shell/render
81	  function) — a saga must never become a scripted slideshow of hand-arranged states.
82	
83	**Animated saga goldens** (recording the motion, not the frames). A per-step frame proves a resting
84	state; a saga can instead be **one animated golden** — an APNG per leaf — recording the real UI
85	*moving* between steps. What keeps it delay-free and deterministic:
86	
87	- **Strip dead delay, keep the animation.** Render time is virtual, so a scripted wait is a run of
88	  *identical* frames — dedup consecutive identical frames and clamp any single hold, so the golden
89	  holds motion, never waiting (a 3 s wait must not become 3 s of golden).
90	- **Lossless, so byte-identity still holds.** Encode APNG, not GIF (whose palette and dithering
91	  aren't deterministic); the comparison stays exact byte-identity and a mismatch writes a per-frame
92	  `expected | actual | diff` to the gitignored failures dir. Capture at a low DPR — lossless costs
93	  no fidelity for it. Flutter reads each frame off the `RepaintBoundary` via `toImage` inside
94	  `runAsync` (the fake-async test zone won't otherwise complete the byte read).
95	- **Mark the gesture.** Paint an expanding ring at each real pointer gesture over the pre-reaction
96	  frame so the strip shows *where* the user acted; programmatic world changes draw none.
97	
98	## 5. Determinism or it isn't spec
99	
100	A rendered expected is only owner-ownable if it is byte-stable forever:
101	
102	- **Pin the clock.** One shared reference time (`REFERENCE_NOW`) threaded to everything that
103	  formats or compares dates; fixture data is authored relative to it. Never wall-clock.
104	- **Fake every nondeterministic input**: network (map tiles, avatars — deterministic generated
105	  substitutes), randomness, platform sensors, locale (pin it; date copy is locale-sensitive),
106	  viewport (one fixed logical size and pixel ratio).
107	- **Load real fonts** in the render harness — test environments default to a glyph-less stub that
108	  renders text as boxes. Load the product's bundled families plus the
109	  icon font; watch for styles that don't inherit the family (button text styles are the classic
110	  leak) — pin the family there explicitly.
111	- **Never wait for "settled".** Indeterminate spinners animate forever; use fixed-duration pumps
112	  so an in-flight state is a capturable, deterministic frame.
113	
114	## 6. Rendering recipes per stack
115	
116	- **Browser-extension / DOM products** (the origin recipe): feed the case's fake data to the real
117	  `render()` in a jsdom document seeded from the real HTML, fold the real CSS on as inline styles,
118	  rasterize with satori + resvg, compare with pixelmatch at **zero tolerated diff ratio**. No real
119	  browser: deterministic and dependency-light, at a documented fidelity tradeoff.
120	- **Flutter**: widget-test golden files are the native equivalent — pump the real app shell
121	  against the fake world and `matchesGoldenFile`; `--update-goldens` is the refresh lane. Load
122	  fonts from the FontManifest (icons included). The fake world (scripted location/auth/backend
123	  that also *records* what the UI asked) is the product's own testing library so the requirements
124	  package and unit tests share it.
125	- Whatever the stack: the comparison is **pixel-exact**. A tolerance is a standing invitation for
126	  unreviewed drift; if a platform renders unstably, fix the determinism (fonts, clock, fakes), not
127	  the threshold.
128	
129	## 7. The gallery is derived output
130	
131	- The spec doubles as a visual gallery: under every image-kind leaf, machine-managed image lines
132	  (tagged with an HTML comment marker) embed the committed goldens — saga leaves get their full
133	  captioned storyboard strip.
134	- A committed **gallery gate** keeps the doc equal to the generator's output byte-for-byte.
135	  Regenerate via the tool, never by hand.
136	
137	## 8. Refresh is a review step
138	
139	One committed refresh entry point regenerates all goldens **and** the gallery together, so they
140	cannot skew. Running it is how an *intended* UI change lands — the refreshed PNGs ride the diff
141	for the owner to approve. It is never how a red case gets fixed: the re-baselining approval
142	procedure (surface actual/expected/diff, ask, only then re-baseline) is canon in the
143	writing-tests skill and the spec-driven-product playbook.
144

1	# executable-requirements pack
2	
3	Active when the repo has `dev/requirements/requirements.md`. The concrete framework standard for
4	running a spec as tests: layout, case naming, the coverage gate's duties, the kind vocabulary
5	(including the storyboard `saga` kind), the machine-managed gallery, and the determinism rules that
6	make rendered expecteds byte-stable. Prose-only: every rule here is enforced by gates **the
7	declaring project itself commits** (coverage gate, gallery gate) — the pack standardizes what those
8	gates must check, not the checking.
9	
10	The judgment layer above it — doc-first discipline, owner-owned expecteds, honest-gap tracking —
11	is not here. This pack exists so a *new* project (or a new stack) adopts the framework by
12	convention instead of re-deriving it.
13	
14	Distilled from three worked implementations in the owner's fleet:
15	missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator (`dev/requirements/` — the origin: jsdom+satori rendering,
16	pixel-exact snapshots), missingbulb/TLDR (adds the cross-tier `server` kind), and
17	missingbulb/ShoutsAndWhispers (`dev/requirements/` — the Flutter port: golden-file rendering, the
18	fake-world harness, and the `saga` storyboard kind's first implementation).
19	
20	## Rules (`RULES.md`)
21	
22	| Rule | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
23	|---|---|---|---|
24	| A requirement line | medium | complexity | prose: 42 words |
25	| A requirement line is a scannable one-liner | low | complexity | prose: 77 words |
26	| The folder is the kind. | medium | complexity | prose: 41 words |
27	| Artifact expecteds live beside their case | medium | complexity | prose: 66 words |
28	| surface snapshot | medium | correctness | prose: 33 words |
29	| behavior | medium | correctness | prose: 22 words |
30	| logic | low | correctness | prose: 12 words |
31	| saga | low | correctness | prose: 10 words |
32	| per-project kinds | low | complexity | prose: 41 words |
33	| heavy/e2e singleton | medium | performance | prose: 21 words |
34	| Strip dead delay, keep the animation. | medium | performance | prose: 49 words |
35	| Lossless, so byte-identity still holds. | high | correctness | prose: 70 words |
36	| Mark the gesture. | medium | correctness | prose: 30 words |
37	| Pin the clock. | high | correctness | prose: 26 words |
38	| Fake every nondeterministic input | high | correctness | prose: 31 words |
39	| Load real fonts | high | correctness | prose: 51 words |
40	| Never wait for "settled". | high | correctness | prose: 21 words |
41	| Browser-extension / DOM products | medium | correctness | prose: 58 words |
42	| Flutter | medium | correctness | prose: 91 words |
43	
44	## Checks
45	
46	| Check | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
47	|---|---|---|---|
48	| `feature-requirements-first` | high | correctness | check: blocking |

+---
+name: writing-wiki-pages
+description: How a product-wiki page is written and grown — the Key insights header, citation, correction without deletion, the growth log, sample-data, when a pass writes nothing. Loaded for any edit under product-wiki/.
+metadata:
+  force-load-on-file-edits-paths:

+
+# Writing product-wiki pages
+
+The rules a wiki page is held to while it is being edited. Which page to grow and where the
+material comes from is the caller's business — the weekly
+[wiki-growth](../../tasks/wiki-growth/task.md) pass picks from each page's open questions, and
+[explore-link](../explore-link/SKILL.md) is handed a source — and both write under these.
+
+- **Opening a page with what it found.** `## Key insights` leads the page: a few bullets carrying
+  the research's actual conclusions — the numbers, the competitor that already does this, the
+  thing that turned out not to be true — enough that a human who reads only the header
+  understands what was researched and what it means. Not a table of contents ("covers pricing
+  and competitors"), not a teaser. The body is where the reader goes for evidence, nuance and
+  citations; the header is where they decide whether they need to.
+
+- **Writing an insight bullet.** One short line, in ordinary words — no qualifying clause, no
+  citation, no hedge, no jargon a newcomer would have to decode. Prefer the finding that would
+  *surprise* someone who knows the field: the thing that turned out not to be true, the number
+  nobody expects, the competitor who already shipped it. Whether a point is obvious is genuinely
+  hard to call, so **don't agonise — when in doubt, keep it**. A borderline-obvious line costs
+  the reader two seconds; a long, careful line costs them the header.
+
+- **Touching the header after a pass.** It is a current view, not a log. A pass that changes
+  what a page's most important findings are rewrites the header to match — a superseded insight
+  leaves it (the correction and its why stay in the body, per below), and an insight the pass
+  didn't touch stays put. If nothing changed the page's top-line understanding, the header
+  doesn't move.
+
+- **Starting a pass on a page.** Compile once, refine in place: read the target page end to end
+  before researching; `## Open questions` is the backlog — research what it flags as open, thin,
+  or dated, and spot-check an existing citation or two per pass. Never re-derive a claim that's
+  already cited and current.
+
+- **Writing a claim.** Cited, never silently rewritten: an uncited claim doesn't get written. A
+  wrong or superseded claim is corrected with a note of why (and its source), never deleted
+  without trace. Every real change records itself in the page's growth log and updates the open
+  questions in both directions.
+
+- **Attributing a figure you saw in several places.** Recurrence is not evidence of who
+  published it: search snippets quote each other, so a number that recurs across five results
+  is one source repeated, and the firm the snippets name is routinely not the firm that produced
+  it. When you cannot open the report, attribute the figure to the publisher a source
+  explicitly names as its **origin**; when sources disagree about that, say so on the page
+  rather than picking one.
+
+- **Finding nothing citable.** No fabricated growth: most passes find little or nothing; no new
+  citable material → no edit, no log entry, no PR.
+
+- **Adding to `product-wiki/sample-data/`, or a new wiki folder.** sample-data gains a file only
+  when a wiki claim needs one to point to — never test fixtures (anything a test asserts against
+  belongs in engineering's tree). Any folder under `product-wiki/` outside the two reserved
+  names *is* a wiki (the structural classifier), so create one only deliberately, seeded with
+  its required sections; automation refines existing pages, it never invents new ones.
+
+- **Touching `product-wiki/product-requirements/`.** The sink is human-reviewed only, and it
+  never changes as a side effect of wiki work or any unattended pass — a wiki finding that
+  should move a requirement gets a growth-log note (and a repo issue) and waits for a human.
+
+- **Landing the change.** Unattended growth always lands as an unmerged PR — researched claims
+  entering a committed knowledge base need the review gate. The owner phrase **"grow the
+  product wiki"** runs the worker method in-session with full web tooling: same rules, same PR
+  discipline.

- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.

Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.

Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and author the canon packs those facets earn. Use from a canon when a project's evidence shows a facet its shelf does not yet home — the curation stages' pack-writing method, and an owner's when asking what a project has taught the shelf.

- github-actions-scheduling: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees — late fires, dropped fires, the 60-day disable — and how to build and describe scheduled work around it. Use when adding, changing, explaining, or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.

- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- verify-in-production: Decide whether a change that has merged can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own once it is live. Use immediately after the merge, beside the conversation capture — never before, and not on request.
- writing-claudinite-skills: Authoring or changing a skill in the Claudinite corpus — SKILL.md conventions, where a skill's checks and tests live, catalog and pack wiring. Use when creating or editing a pack's skills/<name>/ in the canon; a consumer project's own agent docs are authoring-agent-docs' turf.
- writing-handover-issues: How to write a task list a PERSON will execute — a handover issue, an adoption checklist, a "steps only a human can do" list. Use when filing or editing any issue whose body asks a human to click, set, register or copy something. Not for issues describing work you will do yourself.
- writing-migration-plans: Where a plan and a design live, and how to order a plan's phases so nothing stalls mid-run — the plan is a tracking issue (never a plan document in the repo), the design doc carries only the end state with rationale and alternatives; front-load the out-of-band setup, write ALL the code including the cleanup and take one approval for the stack, then chain every execution step to the verification of the one before it as a queued continuation, size the links (how many PRs, what each one's diff is predicted to touch and the automerge policy that prediction becomes) and write the chain to survive a policy park, a red CI or a PR closed unmerged, and keep the tracking issue append-only while implementing. Use BEFORE writing any DESIGN.md, migration plan, phased implementation plan, rollout or cutover plan — including the moment you are about to create a docs/<initiative>/ file — when asked to run a plan as a chain of ad-hoc tasks, and when working through a plan's tracking issue.
- writing-pack-prose: How pack prose is written — RULES.md rules, SKILL.md bodies and check text in a Claudinite pack, local or canon — brevity, structure, triggerability, findability, and the per-pack references doc. Loaded for any edit of a pack's RULES.md or SKILL.md, and when landing a lesson as prose.
- writing-tasks: The contract a Claudinite task is written to — the declaration's fields, the code-work and agentic phases, the precondition as the only decision point, ordering, and how a work item converges. Use when writing or changing a tasks/<name>/task.json or its worker, or when a task-declaration check fires.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- design: Create a design canvas - a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces - posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.

1	# Brief: extracting rules out of a pack's RULES.md into skills (issue #1662)
2	
3	Repo: /home/user/Claudinite (branch claude/github-issue-1662-35o81e, already checked out). You edit
4	ONLY the pack directories assigned to you: `packs/<pack>/**`. Never commit, never run the whole test
5	suite, never touch `packs/README.md`, `packs/directory.GENERATED.md` or anything under `.claudinite/`
6	— the coordinator does those once at the end.
7	
8	## Before editing anything
9	
10	Read these two skills with the Read tool (the PreToolUse guard holds edits of RULES.md / SKILL.md
11	until they are loaded, and they carry the conventions):
12	- /home/user/Claudinite/packs/claudinite-growth/skills/writing-pack-prose/SKILL.md
13	- /home/user/Claudinite/packs/claudinite-canon-curation/skills/writing-claudinite-skills/SKILL.md
14	
15	Also read the worked example of exactly this conversion: `git show 21c62f0 -- packs/product-wiki`
16	(RULES.md shrank to the two always-on rules; a new `skills/writing-wiki-pages/SKILL.md` took the
17	rest; README's rule table was re-rowed and its Skills table gained a row; pack.mjs version bumped;
18	VERSIONS.md gained a row).
19	
20	## The mechanism
21	
22	A skill is `packs/<pack>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` with YAML frontmatter:
23	
24	```
25	---
26	name: <name>
27	description: <one tight sentence: what it is + "Use when …" the activity that should load it>
28	metadata:
29	  force-load-on-file-edits-paths:
30	    - "**/Info.plist"
31	---
32	```
33	
34	`metadata.force-load-on-file-edits-paths` is optional: include it ONLY for a path-scoped skill
35	(the issue row's Scope says `paths:`). Never use the harness's own `paths:` frontmatter field.
36	Pattern grammar: `**` spans directories, `*`/`?` stay in one segment, `{a,b}` expands, matched
37	against the whole repo-relative path (so `**/Info.plist` = that file at any depth, `functions/**`
38	= a top-level tree). Skill names are global across all packs; the coordinator checked the issue's
39	names are free — use them verbatim. Skill directory name == frontmatter `name`.
40	
41	Caution from the issue: a `paths:` glob that is a GUESS at a member's file naming (e.g.
42	`**/*Audio*.swift`, `**/fetch*.{js,ts}`, `**/*time*`, `**/auth*.{js,ts}`) does not earn a forced
43	scope — prefer a description-only (activity-triggered) skill there, or keep only the platform-fixed
44	names of the row (`manifest.json`, `**/Info.plist`, `**/*.entitlements`, `**/firestore.rules`,
45	`**/template.yaml`, `pubspec.yaml`, `.claudinite-settings.json`, `dev/requirements/**`,
46	`.github/workflows/**`, `package.json`, `**/*GENERATED*` …). Decide per row and report what you chose.
47	
48	## What to do per row of your table
49	
50	1. **Create the skill.** Its body carries the moved rules — keep their substance and wording
51	   (this is a move, not a rewrite; do not add requirements), grouped under short headings where
52	   there are several. A skill may keep the `- **Lead-in** — …` bullet form. Keep each rule's
53	   trailing rationale marker `(n)` if it had one (see references below). Where the row says "into
54	   existing <skill>", append a section to that skill instead of creating one. A skill body needs
55	   no preamble explaining the mechanism; open with the content.
56	2. **Remove the moved rules from RULES.md** — shrink-only. Do not reword the rules that stay.
57	   If removing the rules empties a `##` section, drop the heading too. Do not leave "see skill X"
58	   pointers in RULES.md: the skill's description is what triggers it (the harness carries every
59	   mounted skill's description into the session). Exception: a rule that must fire BEFORE the
60	   session decides to open a file stays prose (issue's caution) — flag any row you judge that way
61	   and leave it.
62	3. **references.md** (only if the pack has one): a `(n)` marker in RULES.md resolves to the entry
63	   `- **(RULES-n)** …`; the same marker inside `skills/<name>/SKILL.md` resolves to
64	   `- **(<name>-n)** …`. So for each moved rule that carries a marker, add (or rename, if no
65	   remaining RULES.md rule cites it) the entry under the skill's key, keeping the number. Never
66	   renumber, never invent a rationale. The blocking `references-integrity` check enforces this.
67	4. **README.md** of the pack:
68	   - The `## Rules (\`RULES.md\`)` table must list exactly the rules that remain in RULES.md, in
69	     order, with exact word counts (`prose: N words`), severity in {critical,high,medium,low},
70	     reason in {correctness,performance,complexity,legal}, label under 8 words. Verify with
71	     `node /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Claudinite/43bfea86-1253-5ffe-af8f-161ab205108f/scratchpad/rule-words.mjs <pack>`
72	     which prints RULES.md's rules with counts and the README's rows; they must match 1:1.
73	     If RULES.md ends up with zero rules, drop the table (and say so in a sentence).
74	   - Add / extend a `## Skills` table: `| Skill | Trigger |` rows,
75	     `| [\`name\`](skills/name/SKILL.md) | <trigger: the activity, or "any edit of X — held by the guard until loaded"> |`.
76	   - One or two sentences below the rules table saying what moved into which skill is welcome
77	     (as product-wiki's README does); keep it short.
78	   - If the issue flags "describe-only prose to delete to a README" for your pack, delete it from
79	     RULES.md and fold what is worth keeping into the README.
80	5. **pack.mjs**: bump `version` to the next `60903.N` (today is 2026-09-03; if it is already
81	   `60903.x` use `60903.(x+1)`, else `60903.1`). Keep it a string.
82	6. **VERSIONS.md**: append one row `| <version> | 2026-09-03 | <what changed, naming the new
83	   skills and that RULES.md shrank to the always-on rules> (#1662) |`.
84	7. **Verify**: `node --test engine-tests/rule-index.test.mjs
85	   engine-tests/pack_loader/pack-conventions.test.mjs engine-tests/pack_loader/path-scoped-skills.test.mjs`
86	   plus `node --test packs/<pack>/test/*.test.mjs` if that directory exists. Then
87	   `node engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs 2>&1 | grep -i -A3 "<pack>\|references-integrity" ` to
88	   see no finding names your pack (other packs' findings are other agents' in-flight work — ignore).
89	
90	## Style
91	
92	- Skill description: one sentence, ≤ ~40 words, naming the activity concretely; it is the trigger.
93	- No comments narrating the edit; no "moved from RULES.md" notes anywhere.
94	- Don't rewrite or "improve" the rules' content. Don't add rules.
95	- Markdown links inside a skill to sibling files are relative to the skill's real home
96	  (`packs/<pack>/skills/<name>/`).
97	
98	## Report back (concise)
99	
100	For each pack: the skills created (name, path-scoped or activity, and the globs if scoped), the
101	count of rules left in RULES.md (before → after word count), any row you deliberately did NOT move
102	and why, and the test/check results.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

- do-later: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked for the queue and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when the owner says "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or otherwise defers a change instead of derailing the session.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and author the canon packs those facets earn. Use from a canon when a project's evidence shows a facet its shelf does not yet home — the curation stages' pack-writing method, and an owner's when asking what a project has taught the shelf.

- improve-comments: Improve the comments in a repo's own source — delete the ones that restate the code or narrate a past edit, correct the ones that have drifted from what the code now does, and add the why where only a reader's guess carries it. Use when designing a larger element (the brief is authored then), when filing a migration plan's chain (the retrospective is its last link), when a merge completes a design-doc'd element, or when defining a new retrospective class for a pack, a repo, or the fleet.

- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
