1	# Working discipline
     2	
     3	- **Starting any requested change** — begin from the *problem*, not the solution, in any
     4	  repository and not just this one. Reach an explicit shared understanding with the owner of the
     5	  problem the change is meant to solve **and** agreement that the requested change is the best way
     6	  to solve it; a different fix, or none, may serve better.
     7	
     8	- **Replying to an owner comment** — open with an explicit classification line,
     9	  `Comment class: correction | feature | process-change | other`, where `other` covers questions,
    10	  approvals and command phrases and a mixed comment names each part. An automation dispatch prompt
    11	  is a comment too: class `other`, in your *first* substantive reply rather than at the end of the
    12	  run. Put the class **alone on the line** and any explanation on the next one: the line is scanned
    13	  for *every* class token on it, so restating the menu declares all of them. A class cannot be taken
    14	  back, and a clean re-declaration further down does not override the first.
    15	
    16	- **Acting on a correction** — you misunderstood something. Repair the shared understanding, then
    17	  rework what the misread already touched; the artifact changes as much as the correction demands,
    18	  but a correction never adds a new requirement or rule.
    19	
    20	- **Acting on a feature** — agree on the requirement, record it in the project's requirements
    21	  document (its executable spec, where it keeps one), write the test that proves it and watch it
    22	  fail, then implement until it passes.
    23	
    24	- **Acting on a process change** — the owner is changing *how* work is done. Land it as durable
    25	  rules in the project's local scope, its own local packs (in Claudinite itself, its packs), routed
    26	  through the mechanism promotion ladder (platform setting → hook → check → skill → prose).
    27	  Promoting a rule into the shared canon is the growth lifecycle's separate call, not the
    28	  interactive session's.
    29	
    30	- **Choosing what goes on that ladder** — only a rule that constrains *how work is done* and
    31	  outlives any one feature; a checkable signature doesn't earn a rule its place. Reject two shapes
    32	  outright: a check that asserts particular code exists or still reads a particular way (it pins a
    33	  point in time), and a rule derivable from the product's requirements (that is a requirement —
    34	  take it to the feature path, the requirements document and the test that proves it).
    35	
    36	- **Landing a rule anywhere on the ladder** — author the assurance first, the check the future
    37	  world must satisfy, execute it and watch it fail, and only then make the fixes that turn it green.
    38	  At the prose rung, where no check can carry an in-flight judgment rule, the equivalent step is
    39	  showing the corpus doesn't already cover the rule before writing it.
    40	
    41	- **Building a mechanism for a behavior** — verify against a real run that it isn't already
    42	  provided.
    43	
    44	- **Building release, deploy, versioning or CI plumbing** — look for the shared pack that owns it
    45	  first; copying a mechanic from a sibling repo is the tell that it belongs centrally. If no pack
    46	  owns it, report the gap rather than author a third copy.
    47	
    48	- **Finishing a change** — watch it work **now**; never park it on "check tomorrow". What a task
    49	  costs is its shelf-life, the time from starting it until everyone can forget about it.
    50	
    51	- **Changing scheduled or unattended machinery** — force a run now (the scheduler's wake lever, a
    52	  `workflow_dispatch`, the fleet-wide force sweep) and watch it to a terminal state rather than wait
    53	  for its next natural run.
    54	
    55	- **Planning a migration** — prefer the design that converges in one forced pass to the one that
    56	  trickles across nightly cycles, accept legacy input at the door so nothing has to wait for
    57	  stragglers, and drive the stragglers with a standing mechanism rather than a phase someone must
    58	  remember to close. Write every phase's code — the cleanup, the destructive tail and every
    59	  legacy tolerance's removal included — before asking for approval, and chain each execution step
    60	  to the verification of the one before it rather than to anyone's memory;
    61	  [writing-migration-plans](skills/writing-migration-plans/SKILL.md) owns that ordering and the
    62	  chain's mechanics.
    63	
    64	- **Adding a legacy tolerance** (a dual read, an accepted old spelling, a shim) — it is
    65	  scaffolding, not a feature: ship it with an advisory that fires where the old shape is still in
    66	  use, and with its removal already a link in the migration's chain, due one stated convergence
    67	  window after that advisory reaches the holders. (2)
    68	
    69	- **Choosing an automerge policy for a PR or a chain link** — write it as a prediction of the
    70	  change's shape, the folders and kinds you expect the diff to touch, and never widen it to fit the
    71	  diff that arrived: a policy that fails is the speed bump that puts a person back on the trail,
    72	  not an error to route around. (1)
    73	
    74	- **Predicting a change that could delete production data or degrade the experience past what a
    75	  later PR undoes** — its policy is `nothing`, whatever its diff class; irreversibility is the
    76	  first of the two things review here exists to catch. (1)
    77	
    78	- **Handing over a change whose diff reached more folders or files than its request implied** —
    79	  say so, and name the abstraction that would have kept it in one place: the reviewer reads which
    80	  folders moved to judge whether the change made sense, and a wide diff for a small ask is the
    81	  growth lesson review is for, not a defect. (1)
    82	
    83	- **When verifying now is genuinely impossible** (an external release window, an upstream fix in
    84	  flight, an effect that only appears once the change is deployed, converged or loaded by a later

    86	  offer to the owner to go and check later. File it with
    87	  [verify-in-production](skills/verify-in-production/SKILL.md), unasked, **once the PR has
    88	  merged** and never before — a PR can be rejected, and a still-open branch can be rewritten

    90	  skill owns both halves — whether this change needs one at all (most don't; a test that ran is
    91	  already the mechanism), and the issue that states what puts the change in production and what
    92	  proves it works there.
    93	
    94	- **Finishing a larger element** — one that earned a design doc or a phased tracking issue — a
    95	  point verification is not enough: schedule the review that comes back once the element has
    96	  lived in production about a week, asking whether it is working, misused, overused or underused

    98	  the metrics that measure them included, never improvised when the review runs.
    99	  [production-retrospective](skills/production-retrospective/SKILL.md) owns the trigger, the
   100	  brief, and the lane's other classes — canon, local-pack and fleet alike.
   101	
   102	- **Receiving feedback that flags a misunderstanding** — check whether the artifact is already
   103	  correct before expanding it; if it is, say so and push back rather than edit.
   104	
   105	- **Writing anything** — size it to its idea: "open one issue" takes a sentence, not three
   106	  paragraphs.
   107	
   108	- **Correcting or auditing an artifact against an authoritative source** — derive the corrected
   109	  version from the *source* before reading the existing draft, then diff against the old draft to
   110	  surface what was actually wrong.
   111	
   112	- **Acting on an approval to merge, ship or proceed** — it applies only *backward*, to the work
   113	  already in front of the owner when it's given, never to anything requested or done *after* it. A
   114	  later follow-up, even a fix to the just-approved change, needs its own explicit approval — and a
   115	  multiple-choice answer is not an approval at all, even when an option's wording mentioned the
   116	  action.
   117	
   118	## Harness-tool contracts
   119	
   120	- **Searching for a tool with `ToolSearch`** — a search that finds nothing is evidence about your
   121	  query, not about the environment. Search the fully-qualified name (`select:mcp__<server>__<tool>`,
   122	  copied off the deferred-tools listing) and try the tool before telling the owner a step is theirs;
   123	  the bare short name returns "no matching tools", which reads exactly like absence.
   124	
   125	- **Calling `Edit`** — the file must have been read *with the read tool*; `cat`/`grep`/`sed` don't
   126	  count. The moment shell output tells you which file you're about to change, read that exact path;
   127	  a narrow offset window satisfies it.
   128	
   129	- **Calling `Grep` with a context flag** (`-n`/`-A`/`-B`/`-C`) — it's silently ignored under the
   130	  default `output_mode: "files_with_matches"`, so the call answers only a match count or file
   131	  list, never the lines you asked for, with no error to catch it. Pass `output_mode: "content"`
   132	  in the same call as any context flag.
   133	
   134	- **Needing exact text from the web** — a summarizing fetch tool is not a source; when the bytes
   135	  matter, `curl` into the scratchpad and read from disk. On a `403` don't retry and don't try a
   136	  sibling URL — attribute the search snippet to the publisher instead of asserting it, and mark it
   137	  for re-verification.
   138	
   139	- **Hitting a sandbox or proxy that denies a fetch** — treat it as a **policy boundary, not an
   140	  obstacle to route around**: don't reach for an open-network runner, an ad-hoc CI workflow or a
   141	  push-triggered "probe", to make the request from somewhere the policy doesn't apply. Answer from
   142	  committed reference material or ask the owner, and say plainly that anything unverifiable is
   143	  unverified. Recognize a fetch tool's own signal for a domain-wide **egress block** (e.g. an
   144	  explicit `EGRESS_BLOCKED` error) rather than reading it as an ordinary publisher `403` — a block
   145	  is domain-wide, so working down a list of alternate sources for the same fact spends the same
   146	  denial again on each one, where a `403` is at least per-site. And never file the gap as
   147	  "re-verify next pass": no later agent pass can close a policy-level block either, so mark it as
   148	  needing a human or an unblocked environment instead.
   149	
   150	- **Scheduling a wake-up with the harness** — pass `prompt`, the instruction the woken turn is to
   151	  act on, on any call that isn't `stop: true`; a no-op flag and a stated `reason` do not exempt it,
   152	  and the call is rejected without it. A rejection leaves no fallback armed, which is what the
   153	  `unattended-agents` skill's re-issue rule is for.
   154	
   155	## Warnings and findings
   156	
   157	- **Seeing a build, test or CI warning** — fix it rather than tolerate it, with a small, targeted
   158	  fix that addresses the *cause* in the same change.
   159	
   160	- **Suppressing a warning** — muting it with a flag (e.g. `--disable-warning`), `eslint-disable`,
   161	  swallowing it — is **not** a small fix and never the quick path. Reach for it only as a
   162	  deliberate, reviewed decision once the real fix has been weighed and rejected, and **carry the
   163	  reason at the site**, on the suppression line or the comment immediately above it; that inline
   164	  reason *is* the review record, so record no second justification elsewhere.
   165	
   166	- **Waiving a finding on *text* rather than code** — try deleting the flagged phrase first; a
   167	  waiver is for a crossing that genuinely must exist.
   168	
   169	- **Working around a finding from a vendored check** — confirm the vendored copy is current first;
   170	  the fix may already exist upstream and simply not be pulled in.
   171	
   172	- **Deferring a warning you can't fix now with a small cause-addressing change** (it waits on an
   173	  upstream release, or the real fix is a larger refactor) — open a dedicated issue unless one is
   174	  already open, then move on. Search for that open one by the **invariant identifier** the finding
   175	  names — the symbol, path or id it is *about* — never the sentence it arrived in: every filer
   176	  paraphrases the message and prefixes its own stage's name, so the wording is the one part that
   177	  differs across filings, and a new branch, PR number or run is not a new finding. Resolving it, by
   178	  real fix or a consciously-chosen suppression, happens in that issue's own change.
   179	
   180	# The task lifecycle
   181	
   182	For every new task:
   183	
   184	1. Create a GitHub issue describing the task before starting work.
   185	2. Develop on a branch; reference that issue number in commit messages (e.g. `Refs #123`,
   186	   `Fixes #123`, or `Closes #123`).
   187	3. Open the PR with a closing keyword for that issue on its own line in the **body** —
   188	   `Closes #123`. That is what fills GitHub's *Development* panel, the link between PR and issue
   189	   that anyone browsing either one follows; `Refs #123` is a cross-reference and links nothing
   190	   there. A PR that must not close its issue — one slice of a longer plan, one of several against
   191	   a tracker — still links: give the slice its own issue and close that one.
   192	4. Update the issue's status (comments / close) as work progresses and when it's done.
   193	
   194	- **Spotting a change that should wait until the work in flight lands** — file it as work that
   195	  comes back on its own rather than doing it now or trusting anyone to remember it: the
   196	  [do-later](skills/do-later/SKILL.md) skill, which queues it behind what it waits on.
   197	
   198	- **Filing anything into the ad-hoc queue** (a deferral, a verification, any marked issue) — it
   199	  asks an unattended session **on this repository** to do the work, so only file what such a
   200	  session can actually do here. A read of another repository or a console is not work it can
   201	  do: that item parks minutes after it is picked, and a park is a person's problem filed under
   202	  a mechanism's name. A public URL is the one exception, and only through the coded
   203	  verification form (`verify-in-production`'s probes) — never by asking a session to fetch it.
   204	  Where the work is out of reach, do it now, hand it to a routine that has the reach, or do
   205	  not file it — and say which.
   206	
   207	- **Filing an issue that belongs under another** — a phase of a plan, a verification of a change,
   208	  a follow-up its parent tracks — attach it as a **sub-issue** (`mcp__github__sub_issue_write`,
   209	  method `add`, `sub_issue_id` the **id** the create call returned, not its number), never only a
   210	  number named in the body. The parent then carries what is still open under it, in the place a
   211	  reader is already looking.
   212	
   213	- **Handing over a step only a human can perform** (flipping a repository or console setting,
   214	  granting a permission, adding a secret) — first confirm you genuinely can't do it yourself, then
   215	  give it **its own issue**, never a note in the PR body, with a checkbox per step, what breaks
   216	  while each is off, and its closing condition. The exception is a step whose home is an artifact
   217	  the human is already editing. How that issue is *written* — the checklist as the whole artifact,
   218	  every explanation below it — is
   219	  [writing-handover-issues](skills/writing-handover-issues/SKILL.md).
   220	
   221	# Engineering practices
   222	
   223	- **Naming a file, module, or symbol** — name it for its scope or responsibility, not the
   224	  technology or mechanism behind it.
   225	
   226	- **Referring to a value from more than one place** — prefer a shared constant or a reference over
   227	  copying it, and generate derived data rather than hand-maintaining it. If you can't, add a drift
   228	  guard: the generic `sharedConstants` check for a plain value, or one that runs the real logic
   229	  against the copy in both directions when the duplicate mirrors matcher or predicate logic. Keep
   230	  the guarded literal itself unbroken, since a value split across a line break is invisible to the
   231	  guard and to a `grep`/`sed` rename alike. Have the guard's own text name the places it watches and
   232	  why the split is forced, and don't also comment the duplication — the guard covers it.
   233	
   234	- **Writing file A so it depends on file B** — say what A needs from B, or that it delegates, and
   235	  don't re-spell how B does its job. If you're about to paraphrase B's procedure, point at B
   236	  instead. This holds for code comments and Markdown alike. The test for whether a detail
   237	  belongs: if that detail changes, does A actually care? A specific that wouldn't force A to
   238	  change — B's cadence, B's file layout, the reasoning behind how B works — is B's detail, not
   239	  A's, and doesn't belong in A even as color.
   240	
   241	- **Committing** — one concern per commit: if two changes could each stand alone, split them, and
   242	  a message that wants numbered items is the split talking. Once a commit has landed, revise with a
   243	  new commit, never a rewrite of that one.
   244	
   245	- **Working with a file a test or tool generates** — put `GENERATED` in its name, and don't
   246	  hand-edit it; change the generator. Never resolve its merge conflict by hand: clear the markers
   247	  with either side, re-run the generator against the merged inputs, and commit that output. Consider
   248	  automating the clear with a `merge=ours` `.gitattributes` entry, and `git rerere` for a conflict
   249	  that recurs.
   250	
   251	- **Writing code that depends on how a platform or runtime behaves** — verify that behaviour
   252	  against authoritative docs or a real run, not a comment or a prior commit's claim.
   253	
   254	- **Optimising** — if the change is meant to preserve behaviour, prove it: hash the full outputs
   255	  of both paths across every branch, fuzzing the inputs that select each, and accept only a
   256	  bit-identical match. If the correctness risk outweighs the speed-up, leave the path alone and
   257	  record that as a deliberate call.
   258	
   259	- **Needing a library for a narrow job** — prefer a built-in, or a few lines. When the assumption
   260	  that justified an existing dependency lapses, drop it.
   261	
   262	- **Answering an edge case a review raised** — first check whether the existing composed rules
   263	  already produce the right answer. If they do, add no production code: pin it with a regression
   264	  test that asserts the contrast case too, plus an accept criterion where you track those, and don't
   265	  re-state it in a comment.
   266	
   267	- **Documenting a procedure** — read the authoritative external docs first and write only what
   268	  they don't carry: our failure modes, gotchas, the exact path we ran. Don't document or recommend a
   269	  path you haven't run, however standard it looks.
   270	
   271	- **Writing code that can silently do nothing** — a swallowed error, a best-effort fallback, a
   272	  probe-gated optimisation, a hint the runtime may ignore — record which path actually ran,
   273	  reading the state back where the platform exposes it. During development, before the solution is
   274	  proven right, add that debugging information first and remove it later. Without the record, a run
   275	  where the capability never engaged is indistinguishable from one where it did and didn't help.
   276	
   277	- **Persisting anything on a user's machine** — put it under the one user-deletable location, and
   278	  extend that location rather than earn a second one. If the platform forces something outside it, a
   279	  registration the OS owns, name that explicitly as the exception.
   280	
   281	- **Changing what the software does with a user's data** — the permission string, privacy policy
   282	  and store listing are part of the contract, so change them in the same commit. Retaining something
   283	  new, opening a listener or adding an outbound connection changes the promise rather than adding a
   284	  field: decide it explicitly and rewrite the disclosure before the code. Expect the claim in more
   285	  than one place — grep the whole surface for the standing absolutes it touches ("no tracking",
   286	  "no cookies", "no external assets") and reconcile every hit.
   287	
   288	- **Driving an external runtime more than once in a session** — a headless browser, a device, a
   289	  REPL, a deploy target — write one parameterised driver into the scratchpad, taking the target,
   290	  the selector and the output path from argv, and re-point it rather than author a throwaway per
   291	  invocation.
   292	
   293	- **Automating something that needs live conversation context** — hook it to an existing human
   294	  workflow event rather than background infrastructure; shell hooks have no conversation access and
   295	  fire per turn, not at session end. Consider changing an existing command's definition — usually
   296	  the cheapest trigger.
   297	
   298	- **Writing the exit path of a pipeline or CI step** — an expected, handled outcome exits clean
   299	  with a comment. Reserve non-zero for genuine breakage.
   300	
   301	- **Piping a long command's output through `tail` (or `head`) to keep it readable** — it discards
   302	  the pipeline's real exit code (`$?` becomes the trailing command's, not the one you're
   303	  checking), so a mid-chain failure goes unnoticed, and any earlier summary lines the truncation
   304	  cut are gone right when you need them. Redirect to a file (or `tee`) instead, read `$?` from
   305	  that same invocation, and grep the file afterward for whatever slice you actually need — never
   306	  re-run the whole thing to re-slice its output.
   307	
   308	- **Killing a process by pattern** — `pkill -f` matches the invoking shell's own command line too,
   309	  so never chain it, and bracket one character of the pattern (`[h]ttp.server 8099`) to break the
   310	  self-match.
   311	
   312	- **Working in a fresh checkout or sandbox** — a setup script may start in the repo's parent
   313	  rather than the checkout, so `cd` in before running anything. A `Cannot find module` there is
   314	  usually an install that hasn't run yet, not a code bug: install and re-run before hunting for a
   315	  code-level cause.
   316	
   317	- **Deciding where a config value or a classification lives** — avoid a default; require the value
   318	  explicitly, or make it structural, derived from where the thing lives. Prefer a structural
   319	  classifier to a hand-set field, and collapse a property tracked in several places into one. When
   320	  automation maintains many copies of a config, have it materialize the explicit value into every
   321	  file it maintains instead of interpreting absence.
   322	
   323	- **Handling a value that can be unknown** — unknown is a state of its own: never encode it as a
   324	  zero, an empty string or a type's default, and don't let a decoder collapse it into one. Keep it a
   325	  missing key or an explicit null, keep the zero for a real zero, and preserve all three states at
   326	  every stage of a pipeline. Treat absence as a permanent shape of the data rather than a gap to
   327	  close, and where two fields claim the same fact, let each mean what its own source said and leave
   328	  the call to the consumer.
   329	
   330	- **Writing a check that scans the repo** — take the file set from `git ls-files` rather than a
   331	  filesystem walk with paths to skip, and remember a brand-new file is untracked until you add it,
   332	  so a green run isn't coverage of it. When scanning for a forbidden token, strip comments first so
   333	  it matches code, not prose — string-aware, since a `//` inside a URL is not a comment. Reuse
   334	  `stripComments` from
   335	  [`engine/checks/helpers/code-scanning.mjs`](../../engine/checks/helpers/code-scanning.mjs); if the
   336	  scan can't import it, inline the same pass and point a comment back at that source. Strip in
   337	  **both** directions — a comment that documents or warns about the banned pattern is exactly
   338	  where a naive check trips over its own reasoning, so a commented-out instance must not count as
   339	  present either. And prove the check silent against the repo's own **real** sources, not only a
   340	  synthetic clean fixture — a fixture spelling the same gap the check has just keeps proving the
   341	  matching, and only a real-tree run can disagree with you.
   342	
   343	- **Writing a comment** — carry the why, or a cross-file relationship the code can't state itself;
   344	  if the code plus a known convention already says it, write nothing. Describe the current state,
   345	  never the edit that produced it: don't explain the change you just made, and don't note what was
   346	  removed or renamed. If a comment narrates a past fix, keep only the part still true of the code in
   347	  front of you. When it must name a path, spell that path in one canonical place and point every
   348	  other mention there.
   349

1	---
2	name: writing-pack-prose
3	description: How pack prose is written — RULES.md rules, SKILL.md bodies and check text in a Claudinite pack, local or canon — brevity, structure, triggerability, findability, and the per-pack references doc. Loaded for any edit of a pack's RULES.md or SKILL.md, and when landing a lesson as prose.
4	metadata:
5	  force-load-on-file-edits-paths:
6	    - "**/packs/*/RULES.md"
7	    - "**/packs/*/skills/*/SKILL.md"
8	---
9	
10	# Writing pack prose
11	
12	Whether a candidate *qualifies* as a rule at all, and which mechanism carries it, is
13	[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)'s call — settle it there before writing.
14	
15	**Start from the foundation:** read the "Write each rule" section of
16	[authoring-agent-docs](../../../basics/skills/authoring-agent-docs/SKILL.md) first — its
17	principles (concrete enough to verify, motivation stated, what to do rather than what not to,
18	the right altitude, emphasis reserved) bind pack prose too. This skill is the pack-specific
19	layer on top of them, and doesn't restate them.
20	
21	## The ration
22	
23	Every rule in a `RULES.md` is paid for by every session in every repo that declares the pack,
24	forever, whether or not it ever applies — so prose is rationed, and the ration is small.
25	
26	- **One sentence per rule, near 40 words**: the trigger, the directive, and a consequence
27	  clause only where the rule cannot be applied without it. A candidate that needs a paragraph
28	  to land has not been understood well enough to be a rule yet.
29	- **An extraction pass adds at most two rules.** If more candidates clear the bar, write the
30	  two strongest and drop the rest — they will recur if they were real.
31	- **Split a rule that carries two situations.** Each situation is its own rule with its own
32	  trigger.
33	- A `SKILL.md` loads only when its activity is under way, so it may carry procedure at length —
34	  but it is still rationed by the same test: every line must change what the reader does.
35	  Method, steps and decision points belong there; anything a session must know *without*
36	  loading it belongs in `RULES.md` or a check, and rationale belongs in the references doc
37	  below.
38	
39	## Shape a rule so it fires
40	
41	- **Keying a rule to its trigger** — open with the act the reader is performing, not the state
42	  of the world the rule applies to. Nobody notices that "a value is unknown"; they notice they
43	  are writing an encoder. A rule keyed to a state never fires, because nothing brings the
44	  reader to it.
45	- **Keying a rule the reader reaches while debugging** — name the symptom that sends them
46	  looking ("A fetch to a host you listed failing in-browser"), not the act that caused it. By
47	  the time the rule is wanted the act is over, and the symptom is what they can see.
48	- **Keying a rule that corrects a misconception** — name what the reader wants ("Wanting
49	  `import`/`export` in extension code"), not the wrong move they might make ("Reaching for a
50	  bundler"). Someone who doesn't yet know the move is wrong won't recognise themselves in it.
51	- **Phrasing that trigger** — use the words the reader would use for the situation, and put
52	  them first and in bold, so the rule is findable by scanning the left margin alone.
53	- **Choosing the unit** — one block per situation, not one bullet per rule. A reader arrives
54	  holding a problem, so give them the whole decision in one place rather than a cross-reference
55	  to three neighbouring bullets.
56	- **Splitting a rule that only makes sense after the one above it** — don't. If the subject
57	  needs a "that" pointing back ("Writing that record"), it is a clause of the rule above, not a
58	  situation of its own. Split when a reader could arrive at the second rule without the first.
59	- **Separating the blocks** — one blank line between rules. The block is what a reader lands on,
60	  and an unbroken run of bullets makes them scan lines instead; the separation costs one token.
61	- **Ordering a file of many rules** — past roughly fifteen, group them under headings naming the
62	  surface each concerns, so a reader scans headings before subjects. A flat list that long makes
63	  every bold subject do the work one heading would.
64	- **Grouping that separates two rules which qualify each other** — add an explicit pointer from
65	  the general rule to its exception, or the general one reads as unconditional. That pointer is
66	  the one sentence a rewrite may add that its source didn't have; name it as an addition when
67	  you report the change.
68	- **Ordering the clauses** — the default first, then the `if you can't` fallback, then
69	  `consider` for an optional aid, then the `don't` that the earlier clauses make unnecessary.
70	- **Choosing modality** — grade it per clause and claim no more than the rule needs. Keep
71	  `never` and `always` for the genuinely absolute and reach for `prefer`, `avoid` or `rather
72	  than` otherwise; escalating a `don't` into a `never` changes the rule rather than rewording
73	  it.
74	- **Naming a mechanism** — name the check, helper or skill that owns the mechanics, and stop.
75	  Its parameters, options and failure modes live with it, and restating them here is a copy
76	  that goes stale. The exception is a mechanism you are telling the reader to *run*, below.
77	- **Telling the reader to *run* something** — ship the literal invocation in a fenced block, not
78	  the file's name. The reader is composing a call rather than looking a mechanism up, so a bare
79	  filename buys a probe every time — the `--help` that prints nothing, then the `cat`, then a
80	  hand-built command. (1)
81	- **Closing a block** — say what the other clauses make unnecessary ("don't also comment the
82	  duplication — the guard covers it"), so nobody adds belt-and-braces.
83	- **Keeping an exception** — an exception that changes what the reader would do is part of the
84	  rule; one that only reassures is padding.
85	- **Cutting a rule's prose** — drop rationale that only restates the rule, examples that
86	  re-express it, and mechanics another document owns. Keep the motivation itself: a consequence
87	  the reader needs in order to apply the rule under pressure earns its clause; rationale the
88	  reader doesn't need at act time goes to the references doc below.
89	- **Auditing a file of rules that already exists** — take each rule and ask what a reader would
90	  get wrong without it. Fold the one whose subject points back at its neighbour; cut the one another
91	  pack already carries, the one a check now enforces (keeping only the half the check can't see),
92	  and the one whose mechanism has since been retired — a rule naming code that no longer exists
93	  teaches a world the reader won't find.
94	- **Rewriting an existing rule** — carry the source's own strength forward. A rewrite must not
95	  weaken a rule, and it must not strengthen one either.
96	
97	## The references doc — where a rule's rationale lives
98	
99	A pack keeps **one** `references.md` beside its `RULES.md`, servicing all of the pack's prose
100	files and its checks. It exists for maintenance and review — the periodic pass that asks
101	whether a rule still earns its place needs the reason it was written — never for daily agentic
102	work: no rule sends its reader there, and no session loads it. So it stays in the repo that
103	owns the pack and never vendors: a member mounting a canon pack receives the rules, not the
104	reasoning behind them, and the pass that reaffirms them runs where the pack lives.
105	
106	- **Adding a rule that has a rationale** — write the brief rule in `RULES.md` (or the skill),
107	  and put the reason in `references.md`. End the rule with the bare marker — `… never a
108	  filesystem walk. (3)` — and nothing else: don't name the references file, don't link it,
109	  don't ask the reader to follow anything. Not every rule needs one; a rule whose reason is
110	  self-evident from its consequence clause carries no marker.
111	- **Writing the entry** — one bullet per entry, keyed by the citing file's own namespace:
112	  `- **(RULES-3)** <reason>` for a rule in `RULES.md`, `- **(<skill-name>-3)** <reason>` for a
113	  line in that skill's `SKILL.md`; the marker in the prose file stays the bare `(3)` and
114	  resolves within its own file's namespace. Write the reason so a future review can **reaffirm
115	  the rule from it**: what would have to be true for the rule to be retired.
116	  - A **workaround** explains the issue with not using it, with the evidence (the failing run,
117	    the error, the measured cost).
118	  - A **technology guideline** cites the original documentation it derives from.
119	  - An **owner decision** carries the language of the request that set it.
120	- **Numbering** — numbers are stable identifiers, not positions: the next entry takes its
121	  file's next unused number, a removed entry leaves a gap, and nothing ever renumbers (a
122	  renumber breaks every marker at once). One entry may serve several rules in its file; a rule
123	  may cite several entries (`(3, 7)`).
124	- **A check's rationale** — the entry points at the check, since a declaration admits no
125	  comment and no new key: `- **(check:growth-write-scope)** <reason>`, same reaffirmation
126	  standard. There is no marker on the check side.
127	- **Removing a rule or check** — remove its entry in the same change, unless another rule
128	  still cites it.
129	
130	The `references-integrity` check holds the mechanism together: every marker must resolve to an
131	entry in the pack's own `references.md`, and every `check:` entry must name a check the pack
132	still carries. The `rule-revalidation` task is the mechanism's consumer — it reaffirms
133	referenced rules and checks against their recorded reasons on its weekly pass.
134	
135	## Migrating an existing pack onto the references doc
136	
137	An existing pack — a repo's local pack, or a shared canon pack worked on canon-side (a member
138	never edits the mounted canon) — migrates opportunistically, one pack per pass, whenever a pass
139	is already editing it. An unmarked rule stays valid forever, so there is no fleet sweep to
140	force and no straggler to chase; the check only judges markers that exist.
141	
142	1. **Create `references.md`** beside the pack's `RULES.md` on its first entry, not before.
143	2. **Work each rule**: keep the act-time consequence clause inline; move review-only rationale —
144	   the evidence story, inline issue ids, a cost the reader doesn't need mid-act — into an entry
145	   and end the rule with its marker. Shrink-only on the rules side: a rule may lose review-only
146	   rationale in this pass, never gain text.
147	3. **Recover the missing reasons from history, source-first**: for a rule that states no reason,
148	   read the commit that added it and that commit's PR and issue *before* re-reading the rule —
149	   derive the entry from the source, then diff against what the rule implied. The commit
150	   message, PR body and issue discussion are where this corpus already keeps a rule's evidence.
151	4. **Never invent an entry.** A rule whose reason can't be recovered stays unmarked — an audit
152	   or the `rule-revalidation` pass judges whether it still earns its place; a plausible-sounding
153	   fabricated rationale would let a future review reaffirm a rule on false grounds.
154	5. **Cover the checks** worth reaffirming with `check:` entries the same way, from their `why`
155	   text and their adding commit's PR.
156	
157	## Evidence
158	
159	The commit and its PR remain the archive — dates, session ids, quoted exchanges and the story
160	of the incident live there, never in the rule. What the references doc takes from them is only
161	the **reaffirmable core**: the reason and the minimum evidence a future review needs to re-test
162	it. Keep a measurement inline in the rule only where the number *is* the argument — a cost the
163	reader wouldn't believe stated qualitatively.
164

2	name: writing-claudinite-skills
3	description: Authoring or changing a skill in the Claudinite corpus — SKILL.md conventions, where a skill's checks and tests live, catalog and pack wiring. Use when creating or editing a pack's skills/<name>/ in the canon; a consumer project's own agent docs are authoring-agent-docs' turf.
4	metadata:
5	  force-load-on-file-edits-paths:
6	    - "packs/*/skills/**"
7	---
8	
9	# Writing Claudinite skills
10	
11	A corpus skill is a harness-matched trigger (frontmatter `name` + a tight `description`, plus `force-load-on-file-edits-paths` under `metadata` where an edit of the files it names must not start without it — the PreToolUse guard holds such an edit until the skill is loaded; never the harness's `paths`, which limits when the skill is offered at all) plus the body the agent needs at usage time — well under 500 lines, and nothing a deterministic mechanism could carry instead (the promotion ladder in [engine/checks/DESIGN.md](../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md) decides). A skill may own the rules that validate its action — `checks.mjs` beside the SKILL.md, one module per rule, with their fixture tests under the owning pack's `test/` mirroring the skill's path; shape and the relevance-first gate in [engine/checks/README.md](../../../../engine/checks/README.md#adding-a-rule). Ownership is placement: the skill lives in exactly one owning pack's `skills/` — there is no skill catalog; the pack's own README names what it bundles. Instruction-writing *quality* — how agents actually follow docs — is [authoring-agent-docs](../../../basics/skills/authoring-agent-docs/SKILL.md)' turf; this skill is the corpus mechanics. (1)

---
name: hermetic-page
description: Making a page render hermetically under a browser driver — the fake https origin fulfilled from disk, host-agnostic routing of vendored assets, fakes as init scripts, the two clock modes, stripping runtime-dependent scripts. Use when setting up or debugging a page's world for a headless run.
---

# Hermetic page

## The page's world is an input — replace all of it

- **Serve the page from a fake origin you fulfil from disk, and abort anything you did not
  name.** Intercepting at the browser needs no server process, no port and no free-port race,
  and it reaches *every* request the page makes rather than the ones an application-level mock
  happens to know about. Make the default arm an abort: a new external dependency then breaks
  the run loudly instead of quietly adding real network to a run meant to be hermetic.

- **Use an `https` fake origin.** Geolocation and several other capabilities exist only on a
  secure origin, and a page served over `http` silently takes the denied path instead. Routes
  are fulfilled before any connection is attempted, so no certificate is involved and nothing
  has to be trusted.

- **Route a vendored third-party asset host-agnostically.** A stylesheet you serve in place of a
  CDN copy still resolves *its own* relative URLs against the host it was served from, so the
  font or image files it references arrive addressed to that CDN. Match those follow-up requests
  on the path alone, on any host, or the sheet loads and every asset it names 404s — which
  renders as a silent fallback rather than an error.

- **Install every fake as an init script, so it runs before the page's first script.** A stub
  installed after load has already lost every call made during boot. Seeded randomness, storage
  seeds, and any API you are replacing all belong there.

- **Give the clock two modes and pick deliberately.** A fixed instant is right for a resting
  state. A requirement about what the *passage* of time changes needs the clock installed and
  paused instead, so the page's timers exist and can be wound forward on purpose — a fixed clock
  has no timers to advance.

## Pages that expect their runtime

- **Rendering a shipped page outside its runtime means removing the scripts that need that
  runtime.** They throw on the first missing global and populate nothing, so the capture is of
  an empty surface that looks like a product bug. Strip them after load and set the state you
  meant to show yourself.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

=== packs/flutter/RULES.md
     1	# Flutter
     2	
     3	## Architecture: ports out of the widget tree
     4	
     5	- **Widgets depend on ports, never on plugins.** Every platform/backend concern (location, auth,
     6	  push, backend calls, the clock) enters the UI as a hand-written abstract interface with pure-Dart
     7	  value types; plugin adapters (`geolocator`, `firebase_*`, `google_sign_in`, …) implement them and
     8	  are constructed **only** in `main.dart`. A plugin type leaking into a screen (a geolocator
     9	  `Position`, a `FirebaseFunctionsException`) is a defect: it silently couples every widget test to
    10	  the plugin's platform channels.
    11	- **Enforce the boundary with a committed import-scan test** (dart:io over `lib/ui/`, `lib/screens/`
    12	  looking for forbidden import prefixes). The analyzer won't stop a convenient leak.
    13	- **Ship the fakes in the package** (`lib/testing/`): scripted fakes for each port that also
    14	  *record* what the UI asked of them, plus a `FakeWorld` bundling them with a pinned clock and the
    15	  real app shell. Both the app's own tests and any sibling test package (e.g. an
    16	  executable-requirements suite) import one fake world — never two parallel ones.
    17	- **Extract the root shell into a widget** (`lib/app.dart`) taking the ports as parameters, used
    18	  identically by `main.dart` (adapters) and the test harness (fakes). Tests must never rebuild a
    19	  parallel MaterialApp — actuals come from the shipped shell.
    20	- **Inject the clock.** Any widget that formats or compares times takes a `Clock` port; relative
    21	  time rendered from `DateTime.now()` is untestable and drifts goldens.
    22	
    23	## Widget tests and goldens
    24	
    25	- **Load real fonts before any golden** — the test binding defaults to the glyph-less Ahem stub
    26	  (text renders as boxes). Parse `FontManifest.json` from the root bundle and `FontLoader` every
    27	  family (strip the `packages/<pkg>/` prefix so plain family names resolve), which also loads
    28	  MaterialIcons; bundle text faces (e.g. Roboto) in the test package's pubspec. Watch for styles
    29	  that don't inherit the theme's family — `ButtonStyle`/`styleFrom` text styles are the classic
    30	  leak; pin `fontFamily` there explicitly.
    31	- **Never `pumpAndSettle` around indeterminate progress indicators** — they schedule frames
    32	  forever and the call never returns. Use fixed-duration pumps (`pump()` then
    33	  `pump(Duration(...))`); this also makes an in-flight state (a spinner mid-send) a deterministic,
    34	  golden-capturable frame. Corollary: after `tap()`, pump **twice** — one frame applies state, the
    35	  fixed-duration pump advances implicit animations (ink ripples, color lerps) past the capture.
    36	- **Anything that fetches must be injectable**: map tile providers, avatar images. Widget tests
    37	  block real HTTP (a 400-returning stub client), so a `NetworkImage`/network `TileProvider` in the
    38	  tree means error boxes, not screenshots. Provide a deterministic in-memory substitute (a
    39	  canvas-drawn `ImageProvider` works and needs no asset files).
    40	- **Fix the viewport per suite**: set `tester.view.physicalSize` and `devicePixelRatio` to one
    41	  phone-shaped size (and reset in teardown) so layout — and therefore goldens — can't drift with
    42	  the harness default.
    43	- **Async lifecycle guards need an epoch counter.** A `start()` that awaits (permission check,
    44	  first fix) can re-arm streams/timers after `stop()`/dispose ran mid-await; bump an epoch in
    45	  `stop()` and bail after every await if it changed. The symptom (leaked GPS subscription after
    46	  sign-out) is invisible in tests that don't await realistically.
    47	
    48	## Toolchain habits
    49	
    50	- **Verify plugin APIs against the installed source, not memory.** Major Flutter plugins break
    51	  their APIs often (google_sign_in v7's `authenticate()`, flutter_map v7+'s options, geolocator's
    52	  settings objects); resolved versions live in the pub cache
    53	  (`~/.pub-cache/hosted/pub.dev/<pkg>-<ver>/lib/`) — read them before writing against them.
    54	- **`pubspec.lock` moving without `pubspec.yaml` moving is version skew, not a dependency change.**
    55	  An app commits its lockfile (only a *library* package gitignores it), so the file is tracked on
    56	  purpose — the thing to keep out of the diff is the churn a local `flutter pub get` produces when
    57	  the installed SDK resolves differently from CI's. Unless you deliberately ran an upgrade, revert
    58	  it: `git checkout -- pubspec.lock`.
    59	- **`flutter analyze` at zero issues** (infos included) is the bar a suite holds; lints that fight
    60	  a deliberate convention (e.g. `file_names` vs. leaf-id case filenames) get disabled narrowly in
    61	  that package's `analysis_options.yaml` with the reason as a comment.
    62	- **Sandboxed/CI runners**: `flutter test` can stall for minutes at teardown on GPU-less containers
    63	  with dropped sockets. The pattern that holds: stream output, kill the process group the moment
    64	  the definitive marker prints (`All tests passed!` / `Some tests failed`), watchdog-kill on output
    65	  silence. On healthy machines plain `flutter test` is equivalent — keep the wrapper thin.
    66	- **The web sandbox ships no Flutter SDK.** Claude Code on the web boots without Flutter, so tests,
    67	  `flutter analyze`, and golden regen can't run until it's installed. Install belongs in the
    68	  environment **image** (built once, snapshotted, reused) — never a per-session hook that reinstalls
    69	  every start. This pack declares that need in its `env` block ([pack.mjs](pack.mjs)); a project pastes
    70	  one generic `environment-setup-command.sh` that runs every active pack's requirement via
    71	  [engine/pack_loader/env-requirements.mjs](../../engine/pack_loader/env-requirements.mjs) and asserts it at session start (see [bootstrap.md](../../bootstrap.md)
    72	  Part 9).

---
name: capture-a-screenshot
description: Taking a clipped capture of an element under a browser driver — clipping at the box instead of an element screenshot, why a bounding box goes stale, rounding the clip to whole pixels. Use when writing or debugging code that screenshots a region of a page.
---

# Capturing a clipped screenshot

- **Clip at an element's box rather than screenshotting the element.** An element screenshot
  scrolls the element into view first, and a scroll dismisses whatever hover or focus opened the
  state you came to capture. A clip moves nothing. For the same reason, open hover-driven UI at
  capture time rather than in a preceding drive step, and settle the scroll position
  deliberately before measuring anything.

- **A bounding box is viewport-space and goes stale.** Drivers scroll an element into view
  before clicking it, so a rectangle measured before a click means somewhere else after one.
  Convert to document coordinates at the moment of measurement, then take the clip from a
  full-page shot so a region below the fold is still inside the rendered image.

- **Round a clip to whole pixels.** A layout rectangle is fractional; letting a fractional clip
  reach the screenshot leaves the rounding to the renderer, and half a pixel either way is a
  different image. Clamp it to the page's own bounds as well — a clip outside the rendered image
  is an error, not a crop.

content.content:
1	---
2	name: writing-pack-prose
3	description: How pack prose is written — RULES.md rules, SKILL.md bodies and check text in a Claudinite pack, local or canon — brevity, structure, triggerability, findability, and the per-pack references doc. Loaded for any edit of a pack's RULES.md or SKILL.md, and when landing a lesson as prose.
4	metadata:
5	  force-load-on-file-edits-paths:
6	    - "**/packs/*/RULES.md"
7	    - "**/packs/*/skills/*/SKILL.md"
8	---
9	
10	# Writing pack prose
11	
12	Whether a candidate *qualifies* as a rule at all, and which mechanism carries it, is
13	[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)'s call — settle it there before writing.
14	
15	**Start from the foundation:** read the "Write each rule" section of
16	[authoring-agent-docs](../../../basics/skills/authoring-agent-docs/SKILL.md) first — its
17	principles (concrete enough to verify, motivation stated, what to do rather than what not to,
18	the right altitude, emphasis reserved) bind pack prose too. This skill is the pack-specific
19	layer on top of them, and doesn't restate them.
20	
21	## The ration
22	
23	Every rule in a `RULES.md` is paid for by every session in every repo that declares the pack,
24	forever, whether or not it ever applies — so prose is rationed, and the ration is small.
25	
26	- **One sentence per rule, near 40 words**: the trigger, the directive, and a consequence
27	  clause only where the rule cannot be applied without it. A candidate that needs a paragraph
28	  to land has not been understood well enough to be a rule yet.
29	- **An extraction pass adds at most two rules.** If more candidates clear the bar, write the
30	  two strongest and drop the rest — they will recur if they were real.
31	- **Split a rule that carries two situations.** Each situation is its own rule with its own
32	  trigger.
33	- A `SKILL.md` loads only when its activity is under way, so it may carry procedure at length —
34	  but it is still rationed by the same test: every line must change what the reader does.
35	  Method, steps and decision points belong there; anything a session must know *without*
36	  loading it belongs in `RULES.md` or a check, and rationale belongs in the references doc
37	  below.
38	
39	## Shape a rule so it fires
40	
41	- **Keying a rule to its trigger** — open with the act the reader is performing, not the state
42	  of the world the rule applies to. Nobody notices that "a value is unknown"; they notice they
43	  are writing an encoder. A rule keyed to a state never fires, because nothing brings the
44	  reader to it.
45	- **Keying a rule the reader reaches while debugging** — name the symptom that sends them
46	  looking ("A fetch to a host you listed failing in-browser"), not the act that caused it. By
47	  the time the rule is wanted the act is over, and the symptom is what they can see.
48	- **Keying a rule that corrects a misconception** — name what the reader wants ("Wanting
49	  `import`/`export` in extension code"), not the wrong move they might make ("Reaching for a
50	  bundler"). Someone who doesn't yet know the move is wrong won't recognise themselves in it.
51	- **Phrasing that trigger** — use the words the reader would use for the situation, and put
52	  them first and in bold, so the rule is findable by scanning the left margin alone.
53	- **Choosing the unit** — one block per situation, not one bullet per rule. A reader arrives
54	  holding a problem, so give them the whole decision in one place rather than a cross-reference
55	  to three neighbouring bullets.
56	- **Splitting a rule that only makes sense after the one above it** — don't. If the subject
57	  needs a "that" pointing back ("Writing that record"), it is a clause of the rule above, not a
58	  situation of its own. Split when a reader could arrive at the second rule without the first.
59	- **Separating the blocks** — one blank line between rules. The block is what a reader lands on,
60	  and an unbroken run of bullets makes them scan lines instead; the separation costs one token.
61	- **Ordering a file of many rules** — past roughly fifteen, group them under headings naming the
62	  surface each concerns, so a reader scans headings before subjects. A flat list that long makes
63	  every bold subject do the work one heading would.
64	- **Grouping that separates two rules which qualify each other** — add an explicit pointer from
65	  the general rule to its exception, or the general one reads as unconditional. That pointer is
66	  the one sentence a rewrite may add that its source didn't have; name it as an addition when
67	  you report the change.
68	- **Ordering the clauses** — the default first, then the `if you can't` fallback, then
69	  `consider` for an optional aid, then the `don't` that the earlier clauses make unnecessary.
70	- **Choosing modality** — grade it per clause and claim no more than the rule needs. Keep
71	  `never` and `always` for the genuinely absolute and reach for `prefer`, `avoid` or `rather
72	  than` otherwise; escalating a `don't` into a `never` changes the rule rather than rewording
73	  it.
74	- **Naming a mechanism** — name the check, helper or skill that owns the mechanics, and stop.
75	  Its parameters, options and failure modes live with it, and restating them here is a copy
76	  that goes stale. The exception is a mechanism you are telling the reader to *run*, below.
77	- **Telling the reader to *run* something** — ship the literal invocation in a fenced block, not
78	  the file's name. The reader is composing a call rather than looking a mechanism up, so a bare
79	  filename buys a probe every time — the `--help` that prints nothing, then the `cat`, then a
80	  hand-built command. (1)
81	- **Closing a block** — say what the other clauses make unnecessary ("don't also comment the
82	  duplication — the guard covers it"), so nobody adds belt-and-braces.
83	- **Keeping an exception** — an exception that changes what the reader would do is part of the
84	  rule; one that only reassures is padding.
85	- **Cutting a rule's prose** — drop rationale that only restates the rule, examples that
86	  re-express it, and mechanics another document owns. Keep the motivation itself: a consequence
87	  the reader needs in order to apply the rule under pressure earns its clause; rationale the
88	  reader doesn't need at act time goes to the references doc below.
89	- **Auditing a file of rules that already exists** — take each rule and ask what a reader would
90	  get wrong without it. Fold the one whose subject points back at its neighbour; cut the one another
91	  pack already carries, the one a check now enforces (keeping only the half the check can't see),
92	  and the one whose mechanism has since been retired — a rule naming code that no longer exists
93	  teaches a world the reader won't find.
94	- **Rewriting an existing rule** — carry the source's own strength forward. A rewrite must not
95	  weaken a rule, and it must not strengthen one either.
96	
97	## The references doc — where a rule's rationale lives
98	
99	A pack keeps **one** `references.md` beside its `RULES.md`, servicing all of the pack's prose
100	files and its checks. It exists for maintenance and review — the periodic pass that asks
101	whether a rule still earns its place needs the reason it was written — never for daily agentic
102	work: no rule sends its reader there, and no session loads it. So it stays in the repo that
103	owns the pack and never vendors: a member mounting a canon pack receives the rules, not the
104	reasoning behind them, and the pass that reaffirms them runs where the pack lives.
105	
106	- **Adding a rule that has a rationale** — write the brief rule in `RULES.md` (or the skill),
107	  and put the reason in `references.md`. End the rule with the bare marker — `… never a
108	  filesystem walk. (3)` — and nothing else: don't name the references file, don't link it,
109	  don't ask the reader to follow anything. Not every rule needs one; a rule whose reason is
110	  self-evident from its consequence clause carries no marker.
111	- **Writing the entry** — one bullet per entry, keyed by the citing file's own namespace:
112	  `- **(RULES-3)** <reason>` for a rule in `RULES.md`, `- **(<skill-name>-3)** <reason>` for a
113	  line in that skill's `SKILL.md`; the marker in the prose file stays the bare `(3)` and
114	  resolves within its own file's namespace. Write the reason so a future review can **reaffirm
115	  the rule from it**: what would have to be true for the rule to be retired.
116	  - A **workaround** explains the issue with not using it, with the evidence (the failing run,
117	    the error, the measured cost).
118	  - A **technology guideline** cites the original documentation it derives from.
119	  - An **owner decision** carries the language of the request that set it.
120	- **Numbering** — numbers are stable identifiers, not positions: the next entry takes its
121	  file's next unused number, a removed entry leaves a gap, and nothing ever renumbers (a
122	  renumber breaks every marker at once). One entry may serve several rules in its file; a rule
123	  may cite several entries (`(3, 7)`).
124	- **A check's rationale** — the entry points at the check, since a declaration admits no
125	  comment and no new key: `- **(check:growth-write-scope)** <reason>`, same reaffirmation
126	  standard. There is no marker on the check side.
127	- **Removing a rule or check** — remove its entry in the same change, unless another rule
128	  still cites it.
129	
130	The `references-integrity` check holds the mechanism together: every marker must resolve to an
131	entry in the pack's own `references.md`, and every `check:` entry must name a check the pack
132	still carries. The `rule-revalidation` task is the mechanism's consumer — it reaffirms
133	referenced rules and checks against their recorded reasons on its weekly pass.
134	
135	## Migrating an existing pack onto the references doc
136	
137	An existing pack — a repo's local pack, or a shared canon pack worked on canon-side (a member
138	never edits the mounted canon) — migrates opportunistically, one pack per pass, whenever a pass
139	is already editing it. An unmarked rule stays valid forever, so there is no fleet sweep to
140	force and no straggler to chase; the check only judges markers that exist.
141	
142	1. **Create `references.md`** beside the pack's `RULES.md` on its first entry, not before.
143	2. **Work each rule**: keep the act-time consequence clause inline; move review-only rationale —
144	   the evidence story, inline issue ids, a cost the reader doesn't need mid-act — into an entry
145	   and end the rule with its marker. Shrink-only on the rules side: a rule may lose review-only
146	   rationale in this pass, never gain text.
147	3. **Recover the missing reasons from history, source-first**: for a rule that states no reason,
148	   read the commit that added it and that commit's PR and issue *before* re-reading the rule —
149	   derive the entry from the source, then diff against what the rule implied. The commit
150	   message, PR body and issue discussion are where this corpus already keeps a rule's evidence.
151	4. **Never invent an entry.** A rule whose reason can't be recovered stays unmarked — an audit
152	   or the `rule-revalidation` pass judges whether it still earns its place; a plausible-sounding
153	   fabricated rationale would let a future review reaffirm a rule on false grounds.
154	5. **Cover the checks** worth reaffirming with `check:` entries the same way, from their `why`
155	   text and their adding commit's PR.
156	
157	## Evidence
158	
159	The commit and its PR remain the archive — dates, session ids, quoted exchanges and the story
160	of the incident live there, never in the rule. What the references doc takes from them is only
161	the **reaffirmable core**: the reason and the minimum evidence a future review needs to re-test
162	it. Keep a measurement inline in the rule only where the number *is* the argument — a cost the
163	reader wouldn't believe stated qualitatively.
164

2	name: writing-claudinite-skills
3	description: Authoring or changing a skill in the Claudinite corpus — SKILL.md conventions, where a skill's checks and tests live, catalog and pack wiring. Use when creating or editing a pack's skills/<name>/ in the canon; a consumer project's own agent docs are authoring-agent-docs' turf.
4	metadata:
5	  force-load-on-file-edits-paths:
6	    - "packs/*/skills/**"
7	---
8	
9	# Writing Claudinite skills
10	
11	A corpus skill is a harness-matched trigger (frontmatter `name` + a tight `description`, plus `force-load-on-file-edits-paths` under `metadata` where an edit of the files it names must not start without it — the PreToolUse guard holds such an edit until the skill is loaded; never the harness's `paths`, which limits when the skill is offered at all) plus the body the agent needs at usage time — well under 500 lines, and nothing a deterministic mechanism could carry instead (the promotion ladder in [engine/checks/DESIGN.md](../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md) decides). A skill may own the rules that validate its action — `checks.mjs` beside the SKILL.md, one module per rule, with their fixture tests under the owning pack's `test/` mirroring the skill's path; shape and the relevance-first gate in [engine/checks/README.md](../../../../engine/checks/README.md#adding-a-rule). Ownership is placement: the skill lives in exactly one owning pack's `skills/` — there is no skill catalog; the pack's own README names what it bundles. Instruction-writing *quality* — how agents actually follow docs — is [authoring-agent-docs](../../../basics/skills/authoring-agent-docs/SKILL.md)' turf; this skill is the corpus mechanics. (1)

1	# Chrome extensions
     2	
     3	> **Releasing, versioning, and Chrome Web Store publication are standardized** — before building
     4	> or changing any release/publish machinery in an extension repo, read the
     5	> [chrome-store-releases standard](skills/chrome-store-releases/SKILL.md) and copy its canonical
     6	> workflows instead of re-deriving them.
     7	
     8	## Service worker
     9	
    10	- **Handing a path to a Chrome API or `fetch` from an MV3 service worker** (`importScripts`,
    11	  `action.setIcon`) — make it extension-root absolute: a leading slash, or
    12	  `chrome.runtime.getURL(...)`. A worker's relative paths resolve against the worker's **own** file
    13	  location, not the extension root, and a bare relative path fails silently — it can abort the
    14	  worker on import, or make an API call reject while the worker keeps running.
    15	
    16	- **Wanting `import`/`export` in extension code** — MV3 loads ES modules natively; don't add a
    17	  bundler just to use them. Declare the service worker `"type": "module"` and load page/side-panel
    18	  scripts with `<script type="module">`; relative imports resolve within the packaged extension.
    19	  Content scripts are the exception — they are classic scripts, below.
    20	
    21	## Content scripts
    22	
    23	- **Assembling a shared global from several injected content-script files** — **augment** it,
    24	  never replace it: merge onto it (e.g. `Object.assign`), not `globalThis.X = {...}`. The files are
    25	  re-injected into the page on every activation (e.g. every popup open), so replacing makes each
    26	  newly-injected file wipe what earlier files already attached.
    27	
    28	- **Accumulating state in a file that is re-injected** (e.g. a list a source pushes into) — reset
    29	  it at load time.
    30	
    31	- **Loading ES module code into a content script** — register a tiny **classic loader** whose only
    32	  statement is a *dynamic* `import(chrome.runtime.getURL('…'))`. A **registered or static content
    33	  script runs as a *classic* script — it can't be an ES module**:
    34	  `chrome.scripting.registerContentScripts` and static `content_scripts` inject their files as
    35	  classic scripts (there is no `type: 'module'` mode, unlike a page's `<script type="module">` or
    36	  the module service worker), so a top-level `import` in one throws
    37	  `Uncaught SyntaxError: Cannot use import statement outside a module` — **in the host page's
    38	  console, not the extension's**. Dynamic `import()` is legal in a classic script, and the module it
    39	  pulls in runs in the same content-script isolated world with the content-script `chrome.*` surface
    40	  intact.
    41	
    42	- **Adding an import to a content-script module** — list that module **and its whole transitive
    43	  import graph** under `web_accessible_resources` (gated to the target origins), or the fetch is
    44	  blocked.
    45	
    46	- **Keeping that `web_accessible_resources` list correct** — have a test walk the import graph
    47	  from the entry module, so a newly-added import can't silently fall out of the list.
    48	
    49	## Permissions and host access
    50	
    51	- **Matching a host with `chrome.events.UrlFilter`** — its host operators are **raw string
    52	  matches, not domain-boundary matches**: `hostSuffix: "example.com"` also matches
    53	  `evilexample.com`, and `declarativeContent`'s `PageStateMatcher.pageUrl` gates an action icon or
    54	  page condition on exactly these filters. To mean *apex-or-any-subdomain*, combine
    55	  `hostEquals: "example.com"` with `hostSuffix: ".example.com"` (the leading dot forces a label
    56	  boundary); never gate a security- or origin-sensitive behavior on a bare `hostSuffix`.
    57	
    58	- **Running a content script on arbitrary third-party pages without an install-time host warning**
    59	  — request access at runtime: declare the origins under `optional_host_permissions` plus the
    60	  (silent) `scripting` permission, call `chrome.permissions.request()` **synchronously inside a real
    61	  foreground user gesture** (Chrome rejects the request from a service-worker message handler), then
    62	  register the script dynamically with `chrome.scripting.registerContentScripts()` — never a
    63	  static `content_scripts` entry.
    64	
    65	- **Starting the service worker when a runtime-granted permission is in play** — reconcile your
    66	  stored enabled-flag against the permission actually granted and re-register (or clean up) to
    67	  match, on every start. The grant can be revoked from `chrome://extensions` out from under you.
    68	
    69	- **A fetch to a host you listed failing in-browser** — `host_permissions` does not bypass CORS.
    70	  Listing a host lets the extension's fetches *reach* it, but the server must still return CORS
    71	  headers for the extension origin (`chrome-extension://<id>`) or the request fails.
    72	
    73	- **Reaching your *own* backend** — don't add a `host_permissions` entry merely for that: if it
    74	  already returns permissive CORS the fetch succeeds without one, and the entry only adds a scary
    75	  install-time host-access warning.
    76	
    77	## Sign-in and tokens
    78	
    79	- **Authenticating an extension to a JWT-validating backend** (an API Gateway JWT authorizer, any
    80	  OIDC-validating server) — obtain a Google **ID token** with `chrome.identity.launchWebAuthFlow`
    81	  (`response_type=id_token`) against a Google Cloud OAuth client of type **Web application**,
    82	  redirect to `https://<extension-id>.chromiumapp.org/` (from `chrome.identity.getRedirectURL()`),
    83	  scope `openid email profile`, and **verify the returned `nonce`**. Pin the extension id with a
    84	  manifest `key` so the redirect URI stays fixed. Do **not** use `chrome.identity.getAuthToken` —
    85	  it returns an opaque OAuth *access* token (no verifiable signature/`iss`/`aud`) that a JWT
    86	  authorizer rejects.
    87	
    88	- **Refreshing a token silently** (`launchWebAuthFlow({interactive:false})`) — request
    89	  `prompt=none`. `prompt=consent` always needs interaction and therefore always fails silently —
    90	  reserve it (or omit `prompt`) for the interactive fallback.
    91	
    92	- **Refreshing silently with more than one account signed in** — pass the remembered account's
    93	  email as `login_hint`; otherwise the provider can't tell which session to reuse and forces an
    94	  interactive account-picker. Persist the non-secret email from the first successful sign-in.
    95	
    96	- **Storing a token** — extension storage is unencrypted, so treat tokens as secrets at rest: keep
    97	  the bearer/ID token in in-memory `chrome.storage.session` (cleared on browser exit) and persist
    98	  only non-secret identifiers (e.g. the account email) to `chrome.storage.local`.
    99	
   100	- **Wanting a token to survive a browser restart** — re-run the silent flow; don't switch to a
   101	  refresh-token flow just for that, which puts a longer-lived credential on disk.
   102	
   103	## Extension UI surfaces
   104	
   105	- **Knowing whether your side panel is open** — have the panel open a `Port` on load and read its
   106	  connect/disconnect as open/closed. MV3 gives the side panel no is-open/close API, and an action
   107	  popup suppresses `action.onClicked`.
   108	
   109	- **Opening the side panel programmatically** — `chrome.sidePanel.open()` needs Chrome 116+, so
   110	  raise `minimum_chrome_version` accordingly.
   111	
   112	- **Putting a menu on the toolbar icon itself** — create it with
   113	  `chrome.contextMenus.create({ contexts: ['action'], … })`; the `contextMenus` permission carries
   114	  **no** install-time warning (unlike a broad host permission).
   115	
   116	- **Recreating those menu items on install or startup** — call `contextMenus.removeAll()` first,
   117	  so they self-heal instead of throwing on duplicate ids when the service worker re-runs its top
   118	  level.
   119	
   120	## Introspecting a service worker over CDP
   121	
   122	- **Awaiting a `chrome.*` callback API inside `Runtime.evaluate`** — don't: they don't reliably
   123	  settle when awaited with `awaitPromise: true` (a hang with no internal timeout). Build the awaited
   124	  signal from plain promises (`fetch`/`OffscreenCanvas`) instead.
   125	
   126	- **Reading a worker value from an injected evaluate** — a bare top-level `function`/`const` isn't
   127	  reachable from one, so expose what the probe reads as an explicit `globalThis.x = …`.
   128	
   129	- **Attaching to a dormant worker** — poll for the global rather than reading it once immediately
   130	  after attaching. A dormant worker has no globals until it re-runs its top level, and attaching to
   131	  it is what starts that.

-- **Every page opens with what it found.** `## Key insights` leads the page: a
-  few bullets carrying the research's actual conclusions — the numbers, the
-  competitor that already does this, the thing that turned out not to be true —
-  enough that a human who reads only the header understands what was researched
-  and what it means. Not a table of contents ("covers pricing and competitors"),
-  not a teaser. The body is where the reader goes for evidence, nuance and
-  citations; the header is where they decide whether they need to.
-- **Terse, plain, and only the non-obvious.** One short line per bullet, in
-  ordinary words — no qualifying clause, no citation, no hedge, no jargon a
-  newcomer would have to decode. Prefer the finding that would *surprise*
-  someone who knows the field: the thing that turned out not to be true, the
-  number nobody expects, the competitor who already shipped it. Whether a point
-  is obvious is genuinely hard to call, so **don't agonise — when in doubt, keep
-  it**. A borderline-obvious line costs the reader two seconds; a long, careful
-  line costs them the header.
-- **The header is a current view, not a log.** A pass that changes what a page's
-  most important findings are rewrites the header to match — a superseded
-  insight leaves it (the correction and its why stay in the body, per below),
-  and an insight the pass didn't touch stays put. If nothing changed the page's
-  top-line understanding, the header doesn't move.
-- **The sink is human-reviewed only.** `product-wiki/product-requirements/` never
-  changes as a side effect of wiki work or any unattended pass — a wiki finding
-  that should move a requirement gets a growth-log note (and a repo issue) and
-  waits for a human. It is the only `product-wiki/` content the rest of the repo may
-  build on.
-- **Compile once, refine in place.** Read the target page end to end before
-  researching; `## Open questions` is the backlog — research what it flags as
-  open, thin, or dated, and spot-check an existing citation or two per pass.
-  Never re-derive a claim that's already cited and current.
-- **Cited, never silently rewritten.** An uncited claim doesn't get written. A
-  wrong or superseded claim is corrected with a note of why (and its source),
-  never deleted without trace. Every real change records itself in the page's
-  growth log and updates the open questions in both directions.
-- **Seeing a figure in several places is not evidence of who published it.**
-  Search snippets quote each other, so a number that recurs across five results
-  is one source repeated, and the firm the snippets name is routinely not the
-  firm that produced it. When you cannot open the report, attribute the figure to
-  the publisher a source explicitly names as its **origin**; when sources
-  disagree about that, say so on the page rather than picking one.
-- **No fabricated growth.** Most passes find little or nothing; no new citable
-  material → no edit, no log entry, no PR.
-- **sample-data and new wikis.** `product-wiki/sample-data/` gains a file only when
-  a wiki claim needs one to point to — never test fixtures (anything a test
-  asserts against belongs in engineering's tree). Any folder under `product-wiki/`
-  outside the two reserved names *is* a wiki (the structural classifier), so
-  create one only deliberately, seeded with its required sections; automation
-  refines existing pages, it never invents new ones.
-- **Review discipline.** Unattended growth always lands as an unmerged PR —
-  researched claims entering a committed knowledge base need the review gate.
-  The owner phrase **"grow the product wiki"** runs the worker method
-  in-session with full web tooling: same rules, same PR discipline.

1	# Brief: extracting rules out of a pack's RULES.md into skills (issue #1662)
2	
3	Repo: /home/user/Claudinite (branch claude/github-issue-1662-35o81e, already checked out). You edit
4	ONLY the pack directories assigned to you: `packs/<pack>/**`. Never commit, never run the whole test
5	suite, never touch `packs/README.md`, `packs/directory.GENERATED.md` or anything under `.claudinite/`
6	— the coordinator does those once at the end.
7	
8	## Before editing anything
9	
10	Read these two skills with the Read tool (the PreToolUse guard holds edits of RULES.md / SKILL.md
11	until they are loaded, and they carry the conventions):
12	- /home/user/Claudinite/packs/claudinite-growth/skills/writing-pack-prose/SKILL.md
13	- /home/user/Claudinite/packs/claudinite-canon-curation/skills/writing-claudinite-skills/SKILL.md

16	(RULES.md shrank to the two always-on rules; a new `skills/writing-wiki-pages/SKILL.md` took the

18	VERSIONS.md gained a row).
